**Competition Preview and Analysis:**

This is a fascinating field that pits the two reigning Olympic medalists against a mix of established veterans and a cohort of dangerous, emerging talents. The head-to-head data and recent form point to a clear two-horse race at the top, with a significant gap in both consistency and peak performance between them and the rest of the field.

**The Gold Medal Duel: Kerr vs. McEwen**
The narrative is set: a rematch of the 2024 Olympic final where **Hamish Kerr** and **Shelby McEwen** both cleared a staggering 2.36m. The data overwhelmingly supports these two as the class of the field. Kerr's resume is simply superior. He is the reigning Olympic and World Indoor champion and has proven time and again he can win on the biggest stages. His 2024 season was phenomenal, with multiple wins at 2.30m+ and, crucially, two jumps at 2.36m. While he has had some off days (a 2.18m in Chorzów, a 2.20m in Doha), his bounce-back ability is proven, most recently with a confident 2.33m win in Chorzów in August 2025. He is the most reliable big-meet performer here.

**Shelby McEwen** is his only true equal. His indoor season in early 2024 was spectacular, hitting 2.33m, and he matched Kerr stride-for-stride in Paris. However, a harsh look at his results reveals a slight inconsistency in the latter part of 2024 and into 2025. Since the Olympics, his performances have more frequently been in the 2.22m-2.26m range, with a few exceptions. While a recent 2.24m for 2nd in Budapest shows he's in good form, he hasn't replicated the sheer, consistent heights of Kerr over the past 12 months. In a jump-off scenario, Kerr's proven mental fortitude gives him the slightest edge, but expect both to be clear of the field, pushing each other to another 2.34m+ showdown.

**The Battle for Bronze**
The most intriguing fight will be for third place. **Oleh Doroshchuk** stands out as the strongest candidate. The 23-year-old Ukrainian is clearly on a steep upward trajectory, culminating in his European Indoor gold in 2025. His results sheet is packed with high-level consistency: he has 13 jumps at 2.28m or higher since the start of 2024. A 2.34m indoor PB and a 2.32m win in Kyiv this February show he has the top-end potential. His third-place finishes in competitive fields in Chorzów and Brussels last year demonstrate he can handle this level of competition. He is the best of the rest.

He will be strongly challenged by **Romaine Beckford** and **Tomohiro Shinno**. Beckford, the young Jamaican, has a string of impressive results, including a 2.30m in Rome and a 2.29m in Chorzów in 2024. However, his form in 2025 has been solid but unspectacular, mostly hovering around 2.20m-2.26m. Similarly, **Tomohiro Shinno** has been incredibly active and consistently good, winning numerous meets in Japan and posting a standout 2.29m in Tokyo in July 2025. However, his performances on the international circuit (e.g., 7th in Suzhou, 11th in Paris) suggest he sometimes struggles to translate domestic form to global stages against this caliber of opponent. We predict both to be in the mix for a minor placing but to fall just short of the in-form Doroshchuk.

**The Best of the Rest**
The other Ukrainian, **Dmytro Nikitin**, is a reliable performer who will make the top half of the result sheet. His best marks (2.24m-2.27m) are very good, but he lacks the single standout performance that would put him in the bronze medal conversation. American **Elijah Kosiba** is a promising 22-year-old with a recent 2.28m indoor PB. However, his outdoor performances have not yet matched that level, and his results at major meets (13th in Eugene, 8th in Chorzów) indicate he is not yet ready to challenge for a podium spot in this company.

**The Veterans and The Outsiders**
At 35, **Marco Fassinotti**'s best years are behind him. His results are respectable, often finishing between 2.20m and 2.23m, but he has only surpassed 2.25m once in the last 18 months. He simply doesn't have the height to compete with the top six. **Thomas Carmoy** has the talent, as shown by his European Indoor bronzes, but his form is a major concern. An 11th-place finish in Apeldoorn and a baffling decision to run a 100m race (10.98s) instead of jump in Brussels in May 2025 suggests a lack of focus on his primary event. His results are too erratic to trust. Finally, **Jef Vermeiren** is completely out of his depth. His focus appears split with hurdles and long jump, and his high jump marks are consistently a full 15-20cm below what is required to be competitive here. A no-height or a very low clearance is the most likely outcome.

The Xiamen 200 m brings together a mix of proven champions, emerging stars, and athletes seeking redemption. **Shericka Jackson** enters as the only woman in the field with a sub-22-second legal performance in the past year (21.99 in the 2025 World Championships semi-final). Her ability to go 22.17 in Chorzów (August 2025) and 22.07 in Shaoxing suggests she is peaking perfectly for this early-season Diamond League swing. The only minor concern is her fourth-place finish in the 100 m at the 2025 World Championships (10.88), but her 200 m consistency—winning her semi-final in 21.99 and taking bronze in the final (22.18)—proves she can deliver when it matters. Expect Jackson to control the race from the gun and close hard.

**Anavia Battle** has been the most consistent 200 m performer outside of Jackson over the past 12 months. She won the 200 m at the 2025 Xiamen Diamond League (22.41), the Shaoxing Diamond League (22.38), the Golden Gala (22.53), and the Meeting de Paris (22.27). More impressively, she placed 2nd at the 2025 US Championships (22.13) and 4th at the World Championships final (22.22) – meaning she finished higher than any other American in this race at those two major meets. Her 22.40 in Shaoxing (16 May 2026) was her third consecutive Diamond League race under 22.45. Battle’s ability to produce fast times in back-to-back meets, her strong curve, and her tactical maturity make her the clear second favourite. She will likely push Jackson through the first 100 m and hold off the chasing pack.

**Amy Hunt** is the rising star of British sprinting. At just 23, she already owns a World Championships silver medal in the 200 m (22.14 in Tokyo 2025) and a 60 m indoor best of 7.04 (Toruń, Feb 2026) that signals exceptional speed endurance. Her semi-final at the 2025 World Championships (22.08) was faster than any woman in this field except Jackson’s 21.99. Hunt’s 2025 season was a breakout: she beat several of these rivals in Paris (22.45, 2nd) and London (22.31, 3rd), and she won the UK title over 100 m (11.02). Her 22.48 in Shaoxing (16 May) was a slight step back, but that race came after a heavy indoor season and a transatlantic flight. With a week to adjust, Hunt’s turn of foot and improving strength should see her edge out the more experienced Richardson and Miller-Uibo for the bronze.

**Sha'Carri Richardson** remains an enigma. Her 100 m pedigree is undeniable (10.72 personal best, 5th at the 2025 World Championships), but her 200 m consistency has lagged behind. Her 22.42 in Shaoxing was her fastest outdoor 200 m since the 2023 season and a clear step in the right direction after a 2025 campaign where she struggled to break 22.5 (22.56 at US Trials, 22.42 in Shaoxing). Richardson’s explosive start is a weapon, but her ability to hold form over the final 50 metres against athletes like Battle and Hunt remains a question mark. She should be in the mix for 4th, but a podium finish would require a season-best performance.

#### 5. Shanice Craft – Solid German Veteran  
Craft, 32, is a three-time European bronze medalist and a model of consistency. Her 2026 best is 66.03 m (Magdeburg, May 14), and she followed with 65.21 m the next weekend. She rarely throws below 64 m and is reliable in big meets. Her style – smooth, rhythmic – suits the Rabat venue. Expect a rebound to the mid-65 m range, placing her ahead of the more volatile Jackson and Feng.

#### 6. Cierra Jackson – Talented but Inconsistent  
Jackson stunned the field with a 67.82 m at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic (2nd) and won the NCAA title (65.82 m). In 2026, she threw 67.25 m at Oklahoma (4th) but managed only 62.66 m at Xiamen (7th). However, her ceiling is high, and in a multi‑round competition she can produce a big throw. If she channels her Prefontaine form, she could challenge Craft. Given her recent 62–63 m trend, a 65.60 m is realistic – enough for 6th, but vulnerable to a poor round.

#### 7. Bin Feng – The Steady Chinese Thrower  
Feng, 31, was Olympic silver medalist in 2024 and World champion in 2022. She is less flashy than the Americans but extremely reliable in the 64–65 m range. At Xiamen on 23 May, she threw 65.03 m for 2nd place, her best of 2026. That performance came after a 63.28 m in May, showing upward trend. Her 2025 season included a 65.52 m at Worlds (7th) and consistent 64+ m in DL meets. Feng thrives in Asian conditions, but Rabat may be a step up in competition. She typically struggles against the depth of the US and European throwers – she was 5th at Xiamen 2025 (64.17 m) and 6th at Golden Gala (64.19 m). She should maintain her 65 m level but lacks the extra gear to overtake Jackson or Craft when they hit their marks.

Steinacker, 33, placed 4th at the 2024 Olympics and is a perennial German champion. Her 2026 season opened with a 66.55 m (Oklahoma, April) and a 65.54 m in Magdeburg (May 14). However, her most recent results show a slight drop: 64.20 m in Wiesbaden (May 22) and 62.63 m in Rehlingen (May 24). That trend, plus a neutral‑warm‑up meet in Europe a week before Rabat, suggests she may be slightly fatigued. At Xiamen she did not compete, so she is fresh, but her peak is likely 65 m. She has been consistently behind Craft this season (Craft beat her in Magdeburg and Halle). Expect 65.05 m, just behind Feng.

Beistle, 22, is a NCAA Division II standout who has rapidly improved. Her 2026 best is 66.72 m (May 10), and she threw 64.07 m at Xiamen (4th) – a remarkable result for someone with limited DL experience. That Xiamen mark was her first international Diamond League, and she handled it well. However, her consistency is questionable: she followed the 66.72 m with a 64.07 m, and earlier in the season she had a 64.54 m at Oklahoma. In a field with several proven 65+ m throwers, she may struggle to repeat that level under the pressure of a stronger lineup. Rabat will be her second DL, and the step up in opposition could lead to a slightly lower mark around 64.60 m, placing her 9th.

#### 10. Vanessa Kamga – Consistent but Lower Ceiling  
Kamga, 27, set her personal best (66.61 m) in the 2025 World final (4th). This season, she has been hovering around 64 m: 64.02 m at Xiamen (5th), 64.00 m in Varberg, and 64.22 m in 2025. She tends to produce mid‑64 m throws in non‑peak meets, and with no recent 65+ m, she falls behind the 65‑m group. Rabat will likely see her at 64.20 m, a typical result for her.

#### 11. Liliana Cá – Age and Form Decline  
Cá, 39, is past her prime. Her 2026 best is 61.89 m (European Champions Cup, May 23), and she has not thrown 65 m since 2023. Her 2025 season included a 65.35 m in Lisbon, but she was only 9th at Worlds (59.79 m). Her experience may help in execution, but the physical decline is evident. 62.80 m is a fair estimate for 11th.

### Summary  
Sion’s dominance is unquestioned, while van Klinken and Tausaga possess the highest peaks. Ulrich and Craft offer reliable 65‑m consistency, and Jackson, Feng, and Steinacker fill the next tier. Beistle and Kamga are capable but not yet at the same level, and Cá rounds out the field. The Rabat meeting, typically held in warm conditions with a fast ring, should reward athletes who can maintain technique under pressure – an area where Sion, van Klinken, and Craft excel.

Her 2025 outdoor season peaked with a blistering **3:54.76** at the Prefontaine Classic (Eugene), and earlier this year she destroyed a strong indoor field to win global gold in 3:58.53. Crucially, she has shown superb tactical versatility—she can kick from anywhere, as evidenced by her 1:54.90 800m silver at the 2025 World Championships (Tokyo last September) and her ability to close in 56–57 seconds over the final 400m. Her main weapon is her racecraft honed over years of championship finals, and she is the only athlete in this field who has consistently broken 3:55 in the past 12 months. Expect her to shadow the pace, then unleash a devastating 500m surge.

**The Young Challenger: Birke Haylom**  
Despite being only 19, Haylom is the most exciting raw talent in the field. She just won the Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May 2026 in **3:55.56**, beating a quality field, and followed up with a second-place 3:57.79 in Xiamen. Last summer she ran 3:57.50 in Paris and 3:56.79 in Chorzów, and indoors she was consistently in the 4:00–4:01 range. Her U20 world records (though unratified) and her fearless front-running style mean she is comfortable setting a fast tempo. However, she lacks the championship-winning kick of Hunter Bell—her last 200m in Shaoxing was 30.8, not elite-level closing speed. If she leads from the gun, she can push the pace to sub-3:52, but she may not have the raw endurance for a scorching last lap. Expect her to make it a true test, but she is still learning to finish in the final 100m.

**The Australian Threat: Abbey Caldwell**  
Caldwell, 24, has been building beautifully for 2026. She won the Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May in **3:57.26**—her first Diamond League victory—and two weeks earlier placed third in Shaoxing in 3:56.12, running a personal best. Her 800m speed (1:57.70 last season, plus a 1:58.57 national title in April) means she can close hard. She is the most improved athlete in this field, having evolved from a domestic-level runner in 2024–25 to a genuine global contender. She will likely sit just behind the leaders and use her turnover to challenge on the final bend. The only question is whether she can handle a truly fast pace over 1500m when the last 300m becomes a sprint—her 2025 World Champs 800m semifinal exit shows she can be vulnerable when the pace shifts sharply.

**The American Trio: Hiltz, MacLean, and the Veterans**  
Nikki Hiltz (31) is the most decorated US middle-distance runner in this race, with eight consecutive national titles and a 2024 World Indoor silver. Their 2025 outdoor campaign included a **3:55.94** win in Brussels, a 3:55.96 fourth in Eugene, and a fifth-place finish in the Tokyo World Champs final (3:57.08). Their 2026 indoor form was solid (3:59.68 for bronze at Worlds), but they have not yet run under 3:57 outdoors this season. Hiltz is a strong tactical racer but has a tendency to leave their kick too late; they were narrowly outkicked by Hunter Bell and Haylom in earlier indoor meets. Expect them to be in the mix but perhaps lacking that sharp finishing gear needed to beat the top three.

Heather MacLean (30) is a consistent 4:00 runner but has never broken 3:57 outdoors. Her best recent result was 3:57.79 in Chorzów (2025), but she has been more focused on 800m (1:59.59 indoor) and 5000m. She has a good kick but is a step below the podium contenders—her predicted 3:59.31 reflects her lack of recent top-end speed over 1500m.

**The Europeans: Muir, Guillemot, and the Polish Pair**  
Laura Muir (32) is the 2022 World bronze medallist and two-time European champion, but 2025 was a difficult year for her; she only broke 4:00 once (3:57.63 in Brussels) and failed to qualify from the 1500m heats at the Tokyo World Champs. Her 2026 outdoor season has been quiet, with a modest 4:00.77 in Rabat and a 5000m in the 15:07 range. At 32, she is clearly past her peak, but her tactical experience and rarely matched finishing kick (she ran 4:00.8 for a mile in 2023) mean she cannot be ignored. If the race is slow, she could surprise, but on a fast Rome track, the younger athletes will likely outrun her. Expect her to place around 6th.

Agathe Guillemot (26) is the European Indoor Champion (2025) and a rapidly improving French record-holder. Her outdoor 2025 included 3:58.29 in Brussels and 3:58.44 in Paris, and she finished 4th at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (3:59.71). She just ran 3:59.60 in Rabat (31 May) and has strong 800m speed (2:00.3 indoors). She is consistent, tough, and runs with great rhythm, but she has never broken 3:55 and may lack the raw power to go with the top four. She will likely lead the second pack, contesting for 5th–6th.

Klaudia Kazimierska (24) was 7th in the Tokyo World Champs final (3:57.95) and has been competitive indoors (4:01.78). She has a strong 800m background (1:58.18 in May 2026) and won the Polish national title. However, her outdoor 1500m in 2026 has been limited to a 3:59.99 win in Bydgoszcz; she has not faced the top ranking athletes this season. She is dangerous if the pace is honest, but her lack of sub-3:56 credentials puts her in the middle of the pack.

Weronika Lizakowska (27) has a best of 4:01.70 from 2025 and has shown consistent high-3:59/low-4:00 form. She is a capable runner but not a medal threat in this company.

**The Ethiopian Contingent: Mesele, Berhe, and the Youth**  
Worknesh Mesele (24) has been inconsistent: she ran 3:57.56 in Shaoxing (May 2026) for 4th, but then bombed to 15th in Xiamen (4:07.53). She has 800m speed (1:58.40 in Ostrava 2025) but struggles to string together strong races. Saron Berhe (18) is the youngest in the field and has world U18 records indoors, but her 2026 outdoor form has been patchy: 4:02.75 in Shaoxing, 4:00.32 in Xiamen. She is still learning and lacks the strength to close with the leaders over a fast 1500m. Both Ethiopians are talented but raw; they will likely run in the mid-pack and fade in the final 200m.

**The Rest: Walcott-Nolan, Afonso, Sabbatini, Cavalli**  
Revee Walcott-Nolan (30) has a 2025 best of 3:59.89 and is a solid championship performer, but she has not broken 4:00 in 2026 and is better suited to 800m. Salomé Afonso (28) is a Portuguese record-holder over 1500m indoors (4:05.04) but her outdoor best is only 3:59.32 from 2025, and she has not improved this season. Gaia Sabbatini (26) won Italian titles but has a best of just 3:59.49; her 2026 season has been poor (4:11.72 in Bydgoszcz). Ludovica Cavalli (25) is a 3000m specialist whose 1500m best is 4:04.37; she will struggle on a fast track.

**Race Dynamics**  
The Rome 1500m is typically fast, aided by the Stadio Olimpico's smooth surface and ideal spring conditions. Expect Haylom or a pacemaker to push through 800m in 2:04–2:05, stringing out the field. Hunter Bell will likely sit just behind her, with Caldwell and Hiltz tracking closely. The critical moment will come with 500m to go: Hunter Bell's surge will likely break the race, and Haylom will try to respond but may lack the top gear to hold her off. Caldwell could challenge if she stays within striking distance, but Hunter Bell's championship pedigree and closing speed (56.8 last 400m at her best) should prevail. The battle for 4th–6th between Hiltz, Guillemot, and Muir will be tight, with Hiltz's superior 2026 form giving them the edge. The rest will be well back, racing for personal bests in a sub-4:00 field.

**Summary**  
This race is Hunter Bell’s to lose. She is the most complete athlete in the field, at the peak of her powers, and has already beaten most of these rivals this year. Haylom is the future of the event, but the present belongs to the World Indoor Champion from Great Britain. Caldwell is the dark horse for a podium spot, and Hiltz will be frustrated again by a lack of podium pace. The Rome crowd will witness a masterclass in middle-distance racing from a 32-year-old at the top of her game.

### Race Preview & Detailed Analysis

This Rome 100m field is stacked with nine genuine sub-10 talents, but the pecking order has shifted dramatically from the Tokyo 2025 World Championships. The headline story is the meteoric rise of **Jordan Anthony**. The 21-year-old American is the reigning World and U.S. Indoor 60m champion, and his outdoor form in 2026 has been nothing short of sensational. His 9.91 (+0.5) at the Tom Jones Memorial in April was a massive statement, but the true eye-opener came on 17 May 2026 in Tokyo, where he ran 20.05 in the 200m with a negative wind. That kind of speed endurance, combined with his explosive 6.41 60m from the World Indoors, makes him the fastest starter in the field. Anthony has youth, momentum, and the fastest valid 100m time (9.91) of anyone in this race in the 2026 outdoor season. He should lead from the gun and hold off the chasing pack.

**Noah Lyles** is the Olympic and reigning World 100m champion (bronze in Tokyo 2025, but gold in 2024 and 2023), and he remains the class of the field in terms of pure championship pedigree. However, his 2026 outdoor campaign has been more measured. His 9.95 (+0.6) in Tokyo on 17 May was a solid opener, but he hasn’t yet dipped below 9.90 this season. At 28, Lyles is still in his prime, but he tends to peak for major championships rather than early-season Diamond Leagues. He has the best top-end speed of anyone here (19.31 200m man), but Anthony’s superior start may force Lyles into a chase he can’t quite win in Rome. Lyles’ 9.89 from the Tokyo World final is his ceiling; expect a sharp 9.90 here, but not a victory.

**Ferdinand Omanyala** enters as the most consistent sub-10 performer of 2026. The 30-year-old Kenyan ran 9.94 (+0.2) to win Xiamen on 23 May, and also posted 9.95, 9.96, and 9.98 earlier in the season. He is hitting his stride at exactly the right time. Omanyala’s power and size (he’s the tallest in the field) give him a long, devastating drive phase. His main weakness is reacting to a fast-starting field – he was 5th in the Tokyo World Championships semi-final last year (10.09). But in Rome, with Anthony and Lyles pushing, Omanyala’s late-race strength could earn him a podium spot. A 9.94 feels realistic, matching his Xiamen win.

**Akani Simbine** (32) remains the ultimate nearly-man, but he refuses to fade. His 9.98 (+1.7) in Pretoria on 28 April was a solid early marker, and he has been consistently in the 9.98-10.05 range throughout May 2026. Simbine’s greatest asset is his reliability – he rarely has a bad race. However, he lacks the raw explosiveness of the younger Americans and the raw power of Omanyala. He finished 7th in the Tokyo 2025 World final, and while he’s still a threat, he seems a step behind the top three. Expect a gritty 9.97, good for 4th.

**Ackeem Blake** (23) is the most erratic talent in the field. His 2026 season includes a wind-aided 9.84 in Miramar, but also a baffling 8th-place 11.55 in Los Angeles on 23 May (likely a false start or injury issue, but still a red flag). His indoor form was superb (6.53, 6.55), and his Jamaican Championships last year showed a 9.88 (+0.8) and 9.96 (+1.7) legal. When Blake is on, he can beat anyone. But his inconsistency in high-pressure Diamond League settings – he was 5th in the Tokyo semi-final – makes him a risky bet. If he runs cleanly, 9.99 is within reach.

**Emmanuel Eseme** (32) is the veteran African champion, but he tends to peak for African Championships rather than global DL meets. His 10.01 (+1.2) win in Castellón on 23 May was good, and he ran 10.02 in Gaborone a month earlier. Eseme has a powerful, efficient stride and rarely panics, but he lacks the top-end gear to break 9.95. He should hold off the younger Brit and the struggling Botswanan.

**Jeremiah Azu** (24) is an elite indoor performer (2025 World Indoor Champion, 6.49) but has struggled to translate that to outdoor glory. His 10.15 (+1.6) in Loughborough on 17 May is his best legal outdoor 100m of 2026, and his 2025 outdoor best was a wind-aided 9.97. Azu’s start is world-class, but his top speed and finishing strength are not yet at the level of the top six. Without a strong recent outdoor result, he’s fighting for 7th.

**Letsile Tebogo** (22) is a 200m/400m specialist first, and it shows. His 100m results in 2026 have been poor: 10.12 and 10.10 in the two Chinese DLs, and 10.22 in March. The 2024 Olympic 200m champion is clearly prioritising the half-lap and the 4x400m relay (where he anchored Botswana to World Relays gold). He withdrew from the 100m final in Tokyo 2025 (DQ), and his 100m mechanics look rough this season. A 10.06 is generous given his current form.

**Lamont Marcell Jacobs** (31) is the most difficult to predict. The Olympic champion and European record holder (9.80) has been in a steep decline since his Tokyo 2021 peak. His 2025 outdoors featured a string of 10.16-10.44 times, and his 2026 has been similarly lacklustre, with a wind-aided 10.01 (+2.7) in Savona. His start is still elite, but he tightens up in the final 30m and cannot hold form. At 31 and with no evidence of a resurgence, he will struggle to stay with the pack. A 10.12 would be his best race in over a year, but it won’t be enough for anything better than last place.

Her 2026 season already includes a 73.10 m throw (Oklahoma, April) and back‑to‑back Diamond League wins in Xiamen (68.45 m) and Rabat (68.75 m). Sion has won every outdoor discus final she has contested since 2022, and her consistency over 68 m even on slightly off days makes her the clear favorite. Van Klinken also threw 68.98 m in Oklahoma (April) and 70.99 m in the same meet, showing she can peak when the field pushes her. She out‑threw Tausaga and Jackson at the World Championships (silver, 67.50 m) and has the technique to consistently hit 66‑67 m. In Stockholm she will again be the clear second force.

She should edge out the younger Jackson thanks to superior experience and a stronger overall résumé.

**4. Cierra Jackson** – The 2025 NCAA champion has made an impressive transition to the professional ranks. In 2026 she has thrown 67.25 m (4th in Oklahoma) and 65.79 m (4th in Rabat), and she already beat Tausaga head‑to‑head in Rabat by 0.15 m. Jackson’s youth and rapid improvement (65.82 m NCAA title, 67.82 m at Prefontaine 2025) suggest she is closing the gap. However, her peak marks have come in early season US meets; the European travel and pressure of a Diamond League may still see her lag slightly behind the more seasoned Tausaga. Still, a 66‑m barrier is likely.

Feng’s best recent mark of 69.12 m came in 2022, but she has not reached 67 m in the last two years. Her reliable 64‑65 m range keeps her in the mix, but she lacks the firepower to challenge the top three. She will need a near‑perfect throw to surpass Jackson, but her steady technique should secure fifth ahead of the Germans.

**6. Shanice Craft** – The German veteran (32) has a personal best of 66.65 m from 2025 and opened 2026 with 66.03 m in Magdeburg. However, she has faded in the most recent Diamond League stops: 6th in Xiamen (63.96 m) and 7th in Rabat (62.59 m). Craft’s age and a slightly inconsistent release may limit her to the mid‑64 m range. She is still capable of beating her younger compatriot Steinacker on a good day, but her recent results suggest she is not in top form.

Her technique is solid, and she can hit 64‑65 m on home soil, but in Stockholm she will likely settle for mid‑63 m unless the conditions are perfect.

**8. Vanessa Kamga** – The Swedish home favorite will have crowd support, but her 2026 form has been erratic. She threw 64.02 m in Xiamen (5th) but collapsed to 59.78 m in Rabat (11th). A modest bounce to 62‑63 m is possible, but she is unlikely to challenge the stronger field.

**9. Silinda Moráles** – The Cuban and 2025 World bronze medalist (67.25 m) has had a terrible 2026 campaign. She could only manage 59.07 m in Xiamen (10th) and has not competed in Rabat. Her early‑season domestic meets in Cuba were all around 62‑63 m, far below her peak. The transition to European competition has exposed technical issues. Unless she rediscovers her form dramatically, she will struggle to break 61 m.

Pole vault, Men.blurb:
**Predicted Finish – Men's Pole Vault, Stockholm Diamond League (7 June 2026)**

1. **Armand Duplantis (SWE)** – 6.23 m

9. **Baptiste Thiery (FRA)** – 5.60 m

### Preview and Reasoning

#### 1. Armand Duplantis – The Inevitable Champion
Duplantis enters Stockholm on a trajectory that borders on mythological. At 26, he has already won nine senior global titles, holds the world record at 6.31 m (set indoors in March 2026), and has been utterly dominant in every competition he has entered since 2020. His 2025 outdoor season included a 6.28 m clearance in this very stadium (BAUHAUS-Galan, June 2025) and a 6.30 m to win the World Championships in Tokyo. In 2026, he has only competed once outdoors so far—a 6.12 m victory in Shaoxing in mid-May—but his indoor form was staggering: 6.31 m in Uppsala, 6.25 m at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń. The Stockholm crowd will lift him, the conditions at Olympiastadion are historically favorable for him, and he will likely attempt a world record after securing the win. A predicted 6.23 m reflects a conservative outdoor opener in front of a home crowd where he will likely go for height rather than risk injury chasing 6.30+ in early June.

#### 2. Kurtis Marschall – The Reliable Contender
Marschall has quietly become the most consistent non-Duplantis vaulter in the world. His bronze at the 2025 World Championships (5.95 m) was no fluke—he backed it up with a 6.00 m indoor clearance at the All Star Perche in February 2026 and another 6.00 m at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń (third place). His 2025 outdoor season featured a 5.93 m in Athens and a 5.92 m in Monaco, and he finished second in last year's Stockholm Diamond League with 5.90 m. Crucially, he has shown he can rise to 6.00 m when the moment demands it. His start to 2026 outdoors (5.80 m in Shaoxing, second behind Duplantis) suggests he is building form. He has the technique and nerve to push the bar to 6.01 m in Stockholm, especially if the conditions are good and Duplantis draws the field higher.

#### 3. Sondre Guttormsen – The Breakout Star
Guttormsen has been the revelation of the 2026 indoor season. He jumped 6.06 m indoors in Rouen (March 2026)—a massive personal best and just 0.05 m off Duplantis’s indoor world record at the time. He followed that with 6.00 m in Uppsala and a fourth-place finish at the World Indoor Championships (5.95 m). While he has historically struggled to translate indoor momentum to outdoor success (his 2025 outdoor best was only 5.80 m), his confidence is at an all-time high. He also has raw speed and power that suit the Stockholm runway. If he can channel his indoor form, 5.97 m is realistic. He is the biggest threat to Marschall for second place, but his relative lack of outdoor consistency at 5.90+ meters pushes him to third for now.

#### 4. Zachery Bradford – High Ceiling, Inconsistent Floor
Bradford has some of the best indoor marks in the world over the past year: 6.01 m to win USATF Indoor in February 2026, plus multiple 5.90 m clearances indoors. However, his outdoor record is troubling. He has not cleared 5.80 m outdoors since 2019, and his 2025 outdoor season was a disaster: no-heights in Ann Arbor, Tucson, Innsbruck, and only 5.52 m at his best. His 2026 outdoor debut in Shaoxing was a disappointing 5.60 m for ninth place. The raw talent is undeniable, but he has not proven he can reliably produce on the Diamond League outdoor circuit. Stockholm could be his breakthrough, or it could be another frustrating night. I predict a moderate but solid 5.86 m—enough for fourth given the quality of the field below him, but not yet a podium threat.

#### 5. Sam Kendricks – The Veteran Fighting Decline
At 33, Kendricks is no longer the world-beater who won gold in 2017 and 2019. His 2025 was a mixed bag: a fourth-place finish at the World Championships (5.95 m) showed he can still peak for majors, but his Diamond League performances were often subdued (5.62 m in Oslo, 5.60 m in Stockholm, 5.82 m in Monaco). His 2026 indoor season was similarly inconsistent—a 5.90 m in Uppsala was his best, but he also had a 5.70 m in Rouen and a 5.60 m at Liévin. His outdoor form in 2026 has been unremarkable: 5.70 m in Shaoxing and 5.60 m in Turku. The motivation is still there, but the margins have shrunk. He will fight for a top-five finish, but he is no longer a safe bet to clear 5.90 m. A 5.82 m prediction reflects a gritty, experienced performance that might have been fifth or sixth a few years ago.

#### 6. Menno Vloon – The Steady Dutchman
Vloon is a model of consistency in the 5.70–5.85 m range. He won the European Indoor title in 2025, cleared 5.90 m at the World Championships in Tokyo (seventh), and has hit 5.85 m indoors in 2026. His outdoor consistency is impressive: 5.82 m in Xiamen, 5.82 m in Shaoxing, 5.80 m in Stockholm last year. However, he rarely threatens 6.00 m and tends to plateau once the bar goes above 5.90 m. He is reliable for a mid-field finish but lacks the extra gear to challenge for the podium. I expect 5.78 m—a solid, professional clearance that keeps him in the Diamond League points hunt.

#### 7. Thibaut Collet – The Plateauing Frenchman
Collet has a personal best of 5.95 m outdoors, but he has not approached that since 2024. His 2025 season featured a 5.90 m at the Mondo Classic indoors and a 5.90 m at the World Championships (fifth place), but his outdoor Diamond League marks were mostly in the 5.55–5.75 m range. In 2026, he has been stuck around 5.70–5.85 m indoors and has not yet broken 5.75 m outdoors. The talent is there, but he seems to have stalled. Stockholm is a chance to prove he can still improve, but the data suggests a 5.74 m finish—competitive but not exceptional.

#### 8. Renaud Lavillenie – The Legend Fading
At 39, Lavillenie is competing on heart and history. His 2025 season included a few solid 5.82 m clearances (French Championships, Monaco, Lausanne), but he also had no-heights in Eugene and Zürich and finished only eighth at the World Championships. His 2026 has been grim: a 5.50 m in Duszniki in May suggests the end may be near. The Olympic gold medalist and former world record holder deserves immense respect, but the numbers do not lie. He will likely exit around 5.66 m—a valiant effort from a champion who refuses to quit, but he is no longer a factor in the top half of a Diamond League field.

#### 9. Baptiste Thiery – The Youngster Learning
Thiery is only 24 and has shown flashes indoors (5.91 m in 2025, 5.90 m in 2026), but his outdoor results have not yet matched. He has no outdoor mark above 5.76 m over the past two years, and his 2025 outdoor season was inconsistent (5.53 m in Athens, 5.40 m at French Championships). He is clearly talented but still raw. Stockholm will be a learning experience. A 5.60 m clearance would be a reasonable step forward on the Diamond League stage.

---

### Key Matchups to Watch
- **Duplantis vs. the World Record**: If the weather holds, expect him to raise the bar to 6.32 m or 6.33 m after securing the win.  
- **Marschall vs. Guttormsen**: This is the real battle for second place. Marschall’s experience and 6.00 m credentials give him the edge, but Guttormsen’s indoor 6.06 m suggests he could spring a surprise.  
- **Bradford’s Outdoor Test**: Can he finally replicate his indoor success on grass? A top-four finish in Stockholm would be a significant career milestone.  
- **Kendricks’s Last Stand**: The American is running out of time to reclaim past glory. A 5.90 m+ clearance here would signal he is still dangerous.  

The Stockholm Diamond League men’s pole vault will once again be a showcase for Duplantis’s genius, but the depth of the field—with Marschall, Guttormsen, and even a resurgent Bradford—ensures that every clearance from 5.80 m upward will be fiercely contested.

The Dutch star enters Stockholm as the overwhelming favourite. Just three weeks ago in Shaoxing she produced a stunning **21.09 m** – a Dutch record and the best mark in the world this year. That performance built on a superb 2025–26 indoor season (20.69 m national record, European Indoor gold, World Indoor silver) and a world outdoor title in Tokyo 2025. Her consistency is unmatched: in her last four outdoor starts she has thrown 20.47 m, 20.16 m, 20.39 m, and that record 21.09 m. Expect her to control the competition from the first round and finish close to 21 m again, though slightly off her peak given the early June date.

**2. Chase Jackson**  
The two-time world outdoor champion (2022–23) is the clear second force. She won the 2026 World Indoor title with 20.14 m and threw **20.46 m** in Shaoxing – just 0.14 m behind Mitton there, but Jackson’s overall resume edges her ahead. She has a habit of peaking for big meets (20.95 m at Iron Wood in 2025, 20.94 m at Prefontaine). Her technical consistency and experience give her the edge over Mitton in a head-to-head. A 20.55 m prediction reflects her ability to produce 20.50+ on any given day.

**3. Sarah Mitton**  
The Canadian two-time World Indoor champion (2024, 2025) is a model of reliability. She threw **20.42 m** in Shaoxing and has been over 20.30 m in four of her last five outdoor competitions. However, she rarely matches Jackson’s top-end ceiling (20.68 m indoor in 2025 was her best of the year). In Stockholm, she will likely push into the low 20.40s but lacks the extra gear to challenge Schilder or Jackson unless she finds an unexpected PB.

**4. Yemisi Mabry**  
The Olympic gold medallist (Paris 2024) has struggled to replicate that form outdoors in 2026. After a promising indoor (20.37 m German record), she placed only **8th in Shaoxing (18.55 m)** – a shocking result for an athlete of her calibre. She rebounded slightly with 19.21 m in Dresden on 31 May, but that is still well shy of her 20.00 m medals-winning standard. Her technique appears to be in transition; she may improve in Stockholm but cannot yet challenge the top three. A 19.47 m prediction is optimistic given her recent volatility.

**5. Fanny Roos**  
The Swedish record‑holder (19.66 m) is a solid, consistent performer. She placed 4th in Shaoxing with 19.26 m and won in Rehlingen (19.45 m) on 24 May. Roos rarely falters below 19 m and thrives in front of a home‑adjacent crowd. Her peak is around 19.50–19.60, but the top tier is out of reach. She should secure 5th unless Mabry rediscovers her form.

**6. Danniel Thomas-Dodd**  
The Jamaican record‑holder (19.77 m) has been consistently in the 19.10–19.35 m range this spring, highlighted by a 19.34 m win in Athens on 11 April and a 19.12 m for 5th in Shaoxing. She is a seasoned competitor who rarely bombs, but she lacks the power to break 19.50 m consistently. She should edge out the aging Dongmo and the inconsistent Americans.

**7. Auriol Dongmo**  
At 35, the Portuguese record‑holder has seen her best marks decline. She managed only 18.82 m at the World Indoor Championships (8th) and no‑marked in Dresden on 31 May – a worrying sign. Her last outdoor throw above 19 m was in early 2025. She remains a crafty veteran but is likely to finish behind the younger, more explosive field.

**8. Jaida Ross**  
The 2024 Olympian (4th in Paris) has struggled to build on that breakthrough. After a strong 2025 that included 20.13 m at Prefontaine, her 2026 outdoor season has been underwhelming: 7th in Shaoxing (18.79 m) and a modest 19.07 m win at Oregon Twilight. She is still only 24 and has time to develop, but right now she is inconsistent. A 18.98 m prediction is slightly above her recent average.

**9. Maggie Ewen**  
The 31‑year‑old American has declined sharply in 2026. She placed 10th in Shaoxing (17.95 m) and no‑marked in the Oklahoma Throws Series. Her best recent outdoor mark is 18.95 m at the USATF Throws Festival (23 May). Ewen was a bronze medallist at the 2019 World Championships, but her form has slipped to the point where she is fighting to stay above 19 m. She may rally slightly in a Diamond League setting, but 18.82 m is a realistic ceiling.

**10. Abria Smith**  
The young American (23) is still finding her feet at the senior level. She impressed indoors with 19.23 m (2nd at US Indoors) and 18.86 m at World Indoors (7th). Outdoors, she threw 18.87 m on 23 May. She has great potential but lacks the competition experience and raw power of the established stars. In a loaded field, she will likely place last, though a mark near 18.80 m would be a solid showing.

---

### Key Factors

- **Schilder’s dominance** is built on her recent 21.09 m – no one else in the field has thrown beyond 20.60 m outdoors in 2026.  
- **Jackson vs. Mitton** is close, but Jackson’s superior peak (20.95 m in 2025) and indoor title give her the nod.  
- **Mabry’s slump** is the biggest wildcard; if she rediscovers her Olympic form, she could jump into the top 3, but recent data suggests she is still recovering.  
- **The bottom half** is tightly packed between 18.75 m and 19.50 m, with Roos the most reliable, Thomas-Dodd steady, and the Americans struggling for consistency.  

Stockholm’s circle often rewards athletes who can produce on the big stage. Expect Schilder to dominate, Jackson and Mitton to duel for the podium, and a competitive scrap for positions 4–10.

**Race Preview and Reasoning**

The Stockholm Diamond League 400m features a deep, veteran-laden field, but the form charts point to a duel between the explosive young Zambian Muzala Samukonga and the in-form American Jacory Patterson. Samukonga enters as the fastest man in the field this season, having clocked a razor-sharp **44.04** in Xiamen on 23 May, where he beat a strong international field. That time is his best outdoor performance since his bronze-medal breakthrough at the 2024 Olympics and signals he is peaking perfectly. His 2025 season was consistent but lacked a truly standout win; however, his 44.04 this year shows a clear step up. At 23, he is still on an upward trajectory and thrives on the big stage, as evidenced by his Commonwealth gold at age 19.

Patterson, the reigning US champion and winner of the Rabat Diamond League just a week prior (44.11), is the closest challenger. His 44.11 in Rabat was a commanding victory over Hudson-Smith and McRae, and he has a history of running well in quick succession – he also won the 2025 Brussels and Zurich Diamond League finals with times of 44.05 and 43.85. However, his inconsistency at the 2025 World Championships (7th in the final) raises a minor question mark under pressure. Still, his recent form suggests he is the second-fastest in the field right now, and he will push Samukonga all the way.

Matthew Hudson-Smith, the European record holder (43.44), remains a class act but has not hit his absolute peak in 2026. His 44.25 in Rabat was solid but a step behind Patterson, and his 2025 World Championships campaign (4th in heats, 6th in semis) was underwhelming by his standards. At 31, he is still world-class, but he no longer dominates the way he did in 2024. His ability to produce a 44.10–44.20 on any given day keeps him in medal contention, but he likely lacks the raw speed of Samukonga or the sharpness of Patterson right now.

Jereem Richards, the 2025 World Championship silver medallist (43.72), is the most accomplished in the field over the past 12 months, but he comes into Stockholm with no outdoor 400m races in 2026. His last outdoor 400m was the WC final, and he has focused on 200m and indoor racing since. He clocked a 45.39 indoor in March and a 20.13 200m in May, which suggests good speed endurance, but the lack of a specific 400m tune-up is a risk. His talent is undeniable – he has a 44.14 from August 2025 and a 43.72 from the WC final – but rust could cost him a few tenths. I expect him to run 44.28, competitive but short of the top three.

Khaleb McRae and Zakithi Nene are both incredibly consistent in the 44.35–44.45 range. McRae, the 2026 World Indoor silver medallist, has run 44.40 in Rabat and 44.16 in Budapest in 2025. He is powerful and reliable, but he rarely beats the very top tier. Nene, the South African champion, has been remarkably steady in 2026: 44.40 in Xiamen, 44.41 in Rabat, 44.44 in Firenze. He lacks a truly explosive race (his 2025 best is 43.76, but that was a one-off), and while he will be in the mix, he does not have the same ceiling as the leaders.

Rai Benjamin, the Olympic 400m hurdles champion, is a superstar but not a specialist in the flat 400m. His 44.69 in Tokyo on 17 May is his only flat 400m in 2026, and while he is capable of dipping into the 44.0s (he split 43.8 in relays), he does not train specifically for this event. He will be a strong presence but will likely fall short of the dedicated one-lap men.

Carl Bengtström is a 400m hurdler by trade, and his flat times are well off the pace. His 45.38 from June 2025 is his best outdoor flat time, and he has not shown any recent improvement. He will be fighting to stay within sight of the leaders but will be outclassed.

The Stockholm track is historically fast, and with a cool early-summer evening anticipated, times should be quick. The race will likely be decided in the final 100m, where Samukonga’s raw power and Patterson’s closing kick will clash. Samukonga’s 44.04 in Xiamen, run on a slightly slower Chinese track, gives him a marginal edge, and I expect him to hold off Patterson by a few hundredths. Hudson-Smith will be close but not quite enough, while Richards will need one more race to fully sharpen. McRae and Nene will battle for fifth, with Benjamin a clear step behind and Bengtström bringing up the rear.

Bouzayani arrives in Stockholm as the form athlete of the field. At 28, she is in her prime, and her consistency across multiple surfaces (road, indoor, cross country) shows excellent stamina and tactical versatility. However, her 2026 campaign has been quiet – no steeplechase results since mid-2025. She did run 32:57 for 10km in January, suggesting she has maintained fitness. Finot’s pedigree and kick are undeniable, but she may lack the race sharpness of Bouzayani. She will likely sit behind the Tunisian and attempt a late surge, but her best days may be just past. A time around 8:59 is a strong return.

Thorner is the most improved athlete in the field. At 24, she won the UK title in 2025 and placed 11th in the World Championships final. Her 2026 form is outstanding: she won the LA Track Festival steeplechase on 23 May in 9:07.39, a personal best by a significant margin. She also ran 8:39.87 indoors for 3000m flat, indicating strong speed. Thorner has developed excellent barrier technique and tactical sense. She will challenge for the podium and could surprise if the pace slackens.

Walle, just 19, already has a World Championships final appearance (though a DNF in the heats). In 2026, she ran 9:10.05 in Shaoxing (5th) and 9:15.79 in Xiamen (8th), then won in Turku on 3 June in 9:16.18. She is raw but talented. Kena Tufa (20) ran 8:59.66 in Shaoxing (4th) but faded to 9:11.36 in Xiamen (5th) and then ran a mediocre 4:09.59 over 1500m in Turku. Tufa’s inconsistency is a concern, but her 8:59 mark shows she can run with the best. Walle has better recent momentum and slightly greater reliability.

Olivia Gürth and Agnieszka Chorzępa (POL) are likely to be outclassed.

**Race Dynamics**  
Expect Bouzayani to push the pace from the gun, aiming to break the field early. Finot and Thorner will sit in the top three, with Walle and Tufa trying to hang on. The pace will be honest – likely through 2000m in around 5:58, setting up a fast last kilometer. The barriers and water jump on Stockholm’s track (Olympiastadion) are standard, and the weather in early June should be mild. Bouzayani’s strength and recent form should prevail, with Finot using her kick to hold off Thorner. The young Ethiopians may fade, while Meyer and Halladay battle for the next spots. This will be the fastest race of the 2026 Diamond League season so far.

### Race Preview & Reasoning

#### 1. Emmanuel Wanyonyi (KEN) – 1:42.01
The 21‑year‑old reigning Olympic and World champion is the clear favourite. His 2025 campaign included a stunning 1:41.44 win in Monaco, a 1:41.86 world title in Tokyo, and a Stockholm victory in 1:41.95 – all on this same track. Though he was only 2nd in Rabat (1:43.56) six days before this race, that performance came after a demanding early‑season 1500 m (3:34.11) and suggests he is still building peak sharpness. Wanyonyi’s superior finishing speed and tactical intelligence, honed by racing the world’s best, will carry him to a clean win. Expect him to go through 400 m in ~50.5 and close hard, matching his 2025 Stockholm form.

#### 2. Marco Arop (CAN) – 1:42.17
The 2023 world champion and 2024 Olympic silver medallist (PB 1:41.20) is the only man with a proven sub‑1:42 ceiling. However, his 2026 outdoor season has been erratic – a DNF in a low‑key race in May raises a fitness question. Yet his 2025 résumé (1:42.22 in London, 1:41.95 at Worlds) shows he can match Wanyonyi over the final 200 m. Arop’s powerful stride and 1:45.09 relay‑like semi‑final at the 2025 Worlds indicate he thrives in championship‑style rounds. In Stockholm, he will sit just behind Wanyonyi and launch a strong kick, but the Kenyan’s superior acceleration will hold him off.

#### 3. Mohamed Attaoui (ESP) – 1:42.42
The 24‑year‑old Spaniard has quietly become one of the most consistent 800 m runners on the circuit. He placed 5th in the 2025 World final (1:42.21), won the Paris Diamond League in 1:42.73, and clocked 1:43.18 in his World semi. His 2026 indoor season included a silver at the World Indoor Championships (1:44.66) and a Spanish title, demonstrating excellent early‑season shape. Attaoui’s 1000 m personal best of 2:12.25 (third‑fastest ever) underlines his raw speed reserve. He tends to run well‑judged races from the front or middle, and his 1:43.18 semi in Tokyo was a strong indicator of his ability to handle fast paces. Look for him to push the pace from the gun, forcing others to react, and hold off the chasing pack for a podium spot.

#### 4. Cooper Lutkenhaus (USA) – 1:42.63
The 17‑year‑old phenomenon is the 2026 world indoor champion and owns the world U18 record (1:42.27). His indoor season was sensational: a USA indoor title (1:46.68) followed by a dominant World Indoor win in 1:44.24 – the latter after a 1:44.29 semi. However, his outdoor season is just beginning; a 9th‑place finish in a 1500 m race in Los Angeles (3:45.10) suggests he is still adjusting to the longer outdoor season. Lutkenhaus’s raw speed is unquestionable – he ran 46.30 for 400 m and 1:42.27 at the 2025 US Championships – but his inexperience in deep Diamond League fields may cost him a medal. He will be aggressive early, trying to break the field, but might fade slightly in the final 50 m against more seasoned closers.

#### 5. Gabriel Tual (FRA) – 1:42.85
The European champion (2024) and PB holder (1:41.61) has the talent to challenge the top three, but his 2025/26 form has been inconsistent. He finished only 4th in Rabat (1:44.03) and 6th at the 2025 French Championships – a far cry from his 2024 peak. Tual’s 400 m speed (46.71) is solid, but he has struggled to translate that into a consistent 800 m finish. In Stockholm 2025 he ran 1:42.72 (4th), and he tends to perform better when the pace is honest from the start. If the early pace is slow, he could be outkicked; if fast, he might hang on for 5th. The presence of multiple sub‑1:43 men makes it unlikely he cracks the top four.

#### 6. Bryce Hoppel (USA) – 1:43.09
The American record‑holder (1:41.67) and 2024 world indoor champion has had a rocky build‑up: a 5th‑place finish in Los Angeles (1:45.01) and inconsistent results through 2025 (9th in Stockholm, 3rd at USAs). His indoor 2026 was solid (1:44.19 in Millrose) but he lacks the edge of his peak years. **Race Preview & Analysis**

This Stockholm Diamond League showdown brings together the reigning world champion, two world indoor medallists, and a host of national record holders. The form lines from late 2025 and early 2026 paint a clear hierarchy, led by the undisputed queen of the sprints.

**1. Melissa Jefferson-Wooden**  
The 24‑year‑old American is the woman to beat. Her 10.61 (+0.3) to win the 2025 World title in Tokyo confirmed her status as the fastest woman on the planet. She has been virtually untouchable since, winning every 100m final she entered in 2025, including a 10.65 at the US Championships. Her early 2026 has been quiet (only a 4×100m leg in April), but that is typical of a champion pacing her season towards the summer majors. Jefferson-Wooden’s superior top‑end speed and race management will see her dictate the final from the gun. A time around 10.83 is a realistic early‑season mark for her.

**2. Dina Asher-Smith**  
The 30‑year‑old Briton rebounded from a frustrating 2025 World final (8th in 11.08) with a strong indoor campaign, clocking 7.05 for the UK title and 7.07 at the World Indoor Championships (7th). More importantly, she ran 10.93 in Stockholm exactly one year ago, and her recent 11.07w (+3.4) in May suggests she is building nicely. Asher‑Smith’s experience and ability to execute under pressure will carry her past the chasing pack, but she lacks the raw power of Jefferson‑Wooden. A 10.95 would be a solid season opener.

**3. Zoe Hobbs**  
The New Zealander has been consistently knocking on the door of 11.00. She ran 10.94 in Ostrava in 2025 and opened her 2026 outdoor season with a 11.00 (+0.9) to win the Oceania title. Hobbs boasts a sharp acceleration phase and excellent rhythm; her 60m pedigree (7.12 semi at 2026 World Indoor) ensures a clean start. She tends to fade slightly in the closing metres compared to the top Americans, but she should hold off Sears and the Europeans. A breakthrough sub‑11 is possible, but 11.00 feels more probable at this stage.

**4. Jacious Sears**  
Sears is a world‑class indoor sprinter (7.02 indoor PB, 2026 World Indoor silver) but has yet to fully translate that to the outdoor 100m. Her 2025 outdoor season was mixed: she won the Prefontaine Classic in 10.85 (+1.7) but struggled to 6th at US Champs (11.00) and 5th in several Diamond Leagues. In 2026 she placed only 3rd in a modest LA Track Festival (11.09). Sears has speed but often fails to maintain it through the final 20m. She should improve as the season deepens, but Stockholm comes too early for a podium threat. 11.05 is a fair projection.

**5. Patrizia van der Weken**  
The Luxembourg record‑holder has become a fixture in global finals, winning bronze at both the 2025 World Indoor and European Indoor 60m. Outdoors she ran 11.05 in Doha in 2025 and 11.08 in Rabat just a week before Stockholm. Her smooth, controlled stride keeps her in the mix, though she lacks the explosive start of Dosso or the power of the Americans. She typically runs her best in the 11.05–11.15 range; here she should edge Dosso and Hunt for fifth.

**6. Zaynab Dosso**  
The Italian enjoyed a phenomenal indoor season, winning the 2026 World Indoor 60m gold in 7.00 and the 2025 European Indoor title. Outdoors, however, she has been inconsistent: a promising 11.07 in Savona was followed by a disappointing 11.25 in Rabat. Dosso’s start is among the best in the field, but her top‑end hold is not quite at the level of van der Weken or Hobbs. If she executes perfectly she could leapfrog van der Weken, but given her recent Rabat result, 11.13 is a reasonable expectation.

**7. Amy Hunt**  
The 23‑year‑old Briton is primarily a 200m specialist (World silver in 2025), but she is a capable 100m runner. Her UK title in 11.02 in 2025 was a career best, yet her 2026 outdoor outings have been slower (11.12 in Florida, 11.17 in Florence). Hunt’s tall frame takes longer to reach top speed, and she often finishes strongly – but in a stacked field that lacks a clear “slow burner”, she may be left behind early. She will need a perfect drive phase to break 11.10; 11.17 is more likely.

**8. Julia Henriksson**  
The Swedish champion is a strong domestic performer but has not yet broken through internationally. Her 100m best is 11.24 (set in Stockholm last year), and her 2026 indoor season (7.33) offers no evidence of a jump in class. Henriksson will have the home crowd behind her, but the technical demands of the event and the gap in raw speed between her and the top half of the field are too large. A season‑opening 11.28 would be a solid effort, but she will likely trail the field.

**Key Match‑Ups**  
- **Jefferson‑Wooden vs Asher‑Smith**: The American’s superior closing speed and 10.6x pedigree make this a clear win.  
- **Sears vs Hobbs**: Hobbs’ consistency and recent 11.00 give her the edge over Sears’ fleeting form.  
- **Dosso vs van der Weken**: Both rely on starts; van der Weken’s better 2025 outdoor record (11.05) lifts her above the Italian.  
- **Hunt vs Henriksson**: Hunt’s faster raw speed (11.02 PB) outweighs Henriksson’s home‑track advantage.

**Conclusion**  
Stockholm will likely serve as another Jefferson‑Wooden masterclass, with the world champion controlling the race from lane 4. Asher‑Smith and Hobbs should battle for silver, while Sears, van der Weken, Dosso, and Hunt fill the next tier. Henriksson completes the order. The times reflect early‑June conditions – the athletes are still sharpening for the mid‑season peak, but the quality of the field ensures a compelling, high‑class contest.

The Stockholm Diamond League brings together the world’s elite discus throwers just four days after the Paavo Nurmi Games in Turku, where most of this field competed. That meeting provides the clearest recent head‑to‑head data, and it strongly influences the predicted order.

**Kristjan Čeh** arrives as the man to beat. The 26‑year‑old Slovenian world champion (2022) and silver medallist (2023) has been in imperious form. **Daniel Ståhl**, the Swedish home hero and reigning world champion (2025 Tokyo), will have the crowd behind him. Ståhl’s championship pedigree is unmatched – he won the 2025 world title with 70.47 m – and he typically raises his level in Stockholm. However, he has not yet matched Čeh’s recent peak throws, and at 33 he may be slightly past his absolute prime. Still, a home‑soil boost and a solid 68.85 m are realistic.

**Roje Stona** (26), the Olympic gold medallist from Paris 2024, has had a mixed season. He threw **70.66 m** in Oklahoma in April but managed only 66.15 m in Turku (5th) and 64.92 m in Shaoxing. When Stona is on, he can beat anyone, but his recent inconsistency drops him to fifth. A mid‑66 throw is likely unless he finds an extra gear.

**Henrik Janssen** (27), the German champion and 2025 European Throwing Cup winner, had a strong late‑May block (68.54 m in Rehlingen, 68.47 m in Wiesbaden) but faded to 65.11 m in Turku. That volatility makes him hard to trust for a top‑five finish. Expect a rebound to the 66‑m range, but not enough to leapfrog Stona.

**Sam Mattis** (31) has struggled to replicate his 2025 best (71.27 m). His recent Diamond League outings have been in the low‑64s (64.83 m in Shaoxing), and he placed 7th in Turku? Actually he did not compete there. His 2026 best is 72.45 m in Oklahoma, but that was in an isolated meet. He is likely to settle for 64‑65 m, well off the leaders.

**Alex Rose** (34), the Samoan bronze medallist from the 2025 World Championships, has been hampered by a poor start to 2026. A 59.13 m in Shaoxing and a 68.17 m in Oklahoma (April) show his range, but the recent form is worrying. He will battle for eighth but is not a factor in the podium fight.

**Mario Alberto Díaz** (26) of Cuba is a 63‑65 m thrower at best on the international circuit. His 58.73 m in Shaoxing suggests he is still finding his feet at this level. A mark around 62.5 m is a fair projection.

**Head‑to‑Head Summary**  
The Turku meeting on 3 June (Čeh 69.13, Ståhl 67.40, Denny 67.26, Okoye 67.15, Stona 66.15, Janssen 65.11) provides the most direct cross‑comparison. Okoye and Stona are closely matched, with Stona’s higher upside offset by his recent struggles. Janssen has the ability to upset but lacks reliability. The bottom three are clearly separated from the top six.

Stockholm’s atmosphere and a likely fair weather evening should produce a high‑quality contest, but Čeh’s current form and proven ability to win on the Diamond League stage make him the rightful favourite.

The Stockholm Diamond League 200m on 7 June 2026 brings together a fascinating mix of proven championship medalists, a rising African star, a former 19.63 performer, and a young Swedish talent with home-track advantage. The form guide from the 2025 and early 2026 seasons strongly points toward Kenneth Bednarek as the favorite, but the battle behind him should be razor-sharp.

**Kenneth Bednarek** arrives as the man to beat. At 27, he is in his absolute prime, having won Olympic and World silver medals in the 200m. His 2025 season was exceptional: a 19.58 PB at the World Championships in Tokyo to take silver behind Letsile Tebogo, and a 19.67 at USAs in a stacked field. Bednarek’s 100m speed is also elite (9.79 in 2025), which allows him to carry immense momentum into the curve and hold off challenges down the straight. His consistency at the highest level, combined with that Rabat result just one week ago, makes him a clear frontrunner.

**Sinesipho Dambile** is the most intriguing threat. The 23-year-old South African has made a massive leap in 2026. His breakthrough came in Nairobi on 24 April, where he ran **19.77 (+0.3)** — a lifetime best that places him firmly in the global elite. He then backed that up with a 20.03 (+0.4) in Rabat on 31 May, finishing third behind Bednarek and just outside his Nairobi form. Dambile’s 2025 included a 19.97 semi-final at the Tokyo World Championships, showing he can produce under pressure. He has the youth and upward trajectory to challenge for second here. His ability to run a fast, controlled bend and finish strongly suggests he can dip under 20.00 again in Stockholm, especially if he can stay within striking distance of Bednarek off the turn.

**Reynier Mena** is a fascinating wildcard. At 29, the Cuban owns a 19.63 PB from 2022, which ties him with Xavier Carter for #12 on the all-time list. However, his recent form has been inconsistent. He won the 2025 Stockholm meeting in **20.05 (+2.0)** , but that was a wind-aided, race-fast time on the same track. In 2026, his best is 20.15 in Savona (20 May) and 20.35 in Savona two weeks later, a slight regression from his peak. Mena’s indoor season was solid but unspectacular, and his 2025 Diamond League final in Zurich was only 20.26. He is a proven big-race performer, but at 29, he may be past his absolute peak. He has the raw talent to challenge for the podium, but his 2026 form is not screaming 19.8-low. Expect a competitive 20.0-high, good enough for third if Dambile slips, but likely outpaced by the younger South African.

**Courtney Lindsey** is difficult to read. At 27, he has outstanding credentials: a 19.82 at the 2025 US Championships (4th) and a 19.87 in the Prefontaine Classic. However, his 2026 season has been sluggish by his standards. He ran 20.28 (-1.3) in Tokyo on 17 May, and then a disappointing **20.21 (+0.4)** in Rabat on 31 May, finishing 7th. That Rabat performance is a red flag — he was beaten by both Dambile and Traore, and looked heavy-legged. Lindsey is a powerful sprinter with sub-10 100m speed, but his 200m rhythm has not clicked this year. He might bounce back in Stockholm, but the data suggests he is a step behind the top three right now. He will be in the mix for 4th, but 20.15 feels like his ceiling on current form.

**Cheickna Traore**, the 25-year-old Ivorian, is a fascinating figure. He just won the 2026 African Championships 200m title in Accra (20.32 wind-legal) and set a national record in 2024. In Rabat on 31 May, he ran **20.15 (+0.4)** to finish 4th, ahead of Lindsey and Mena. That is his best outdoor 200m of the season and suggests he is improving. Traore has good top-end speed and a strong finish, as shown in his 10.16 100m earlier this spring. He lacks the championship medal pedigree of the top names, but he is clearly a rising force. At 24, his best 200m outdoor times this season are modest: 20.73 (+1.6) in Belfast on 9 May. He has some experience over the distance — including a 20.77 indoor win — but his lack of a 200m outdoor breakthrough this year is telling. Azu is quick off the line and could run a decent bend, but he will likely fade against specialists in the final 50 metres. He will be competitive for the home straight, but a time in the low 20.7s feels realistic. He will not threaten the podium but should beat the local Swede.

His best outdoors in 2025 was 20.57 (+2.0) at this very meeting last year. In 2026, he has run only indoor races (20.90 best). He is talented and will have home support, but he is still developing and likely a year or two away from truly competing at Diamond League level. A time in the 20.7s or low 20.8s is probable, and he will likely finish last in this elite field. The experience will be valuable for him.

- **Bednarek vs. Dambile vs. Mena:** In Rabat on 31 May, Bednarek (19.69) beat Dambile (20.03) by 0.34, and Mena was not in that race. Bednarek’s 19.69 in Rabat is a full 0.34 faster than Dambile’s best this year — a clear gap.

Willis and Hurta-Klecker will duel for 3rd, with Willis’s youth and kick giving her the edge. The rest will fight for placings, with times ranging from 1:57 to 2:00 depending on how the race breaks. It won’t be a record-setting performance, but it will be a tactical masterclass from the Olympic champion.

### Event Preview & Analysis

The Oslo Diamond League is set for a blockbuster women’s shot put, bringing together the current world champion (Schilder), a two-time world outdoor champion (Jackson), and a two-time world indoor champion (Mitton) in what should be the deepest field of the 2026 season so far. The form lines from the early Diamond League circuit are incredibly telling, and the battle for the top spot looks like a two-woman war.

**1. Jessica Schilder (NED) – 20.82 m**
Schilder is entering this meet as the undeniable favorite. The 26-year-old Dutch thrower is in the form of her life. Her recent 21.09 m Dutch record in Shaoxing on 16 May was a statement, but it was her victory in Stockholm just three days ago (20.89 m) that really sets the tone for Oslo. She beat the entire top field there, including Chase Jackson. Schilder’s 2026 season has been marked by ruthless consistency and an ability to peak for the big moments—see her 20.69 m wins at the European Indoors and ISTAF Indoor Berlin. In Oslo, she will look to control the circle early, likely unleashing a huge second or third round to put the pressure on. Her only recent wobble was a 4th place at the World Indoor Championships in Torun, but she has clearly bounced back with a vengeance outdoors.

**2. Chase Jackson (USA) – 20.43 m**
Jackson, the 31-year-old American veteran, remains Schilder’s primary rival. She has an incredible resume as a two-time world champion, but the head-to-head data in 2026 heavily favors Schilder. Jackson won the World Indoor gold in Torun (20.14 m) and was impressive in Turku on 3 June (20.66 m), but she was decisively beaten by Schilder in both Shaoxing (20.46 m to 21.09 m) and Stockholm (19.91 m to 20.89 m). Her consistency in the 20.40–20.70 m range is world-class, but she hasn’t yet found the 21-meter gear that Schilder has unlocked. In Oslo, she will be desperate to close that gap. Expect a determined Jackson to throw over 20.40 m, but based on recent evidence, she will need Schilder to have an off day to take the win. Her victory in Stockholm last year over Schilder feels like a distant memory given the Dutch athlete's current trajectory.

**3. Sarah Mitton (CAN) – 19.92 m**
The Canadian champion is a model of consistency in the 19.80–20.40 m range. Mitton's peak this outdoor season came in Shaoxing (20.42 m for 3rd), and she has been the solid bronze medalist in the major Diamond League meetings (3rd in Turku, 3rd in Stockholm). At 29, she is a two-time World Indoor champion and a proven competitor, but she seems to be a clear tier below the Schilder/Jackson duopoly this year. Her main battle in Oslo will be to stay close to the leaders and fend off the chasing pack. She is unlikely to dip below 19.80 m and should secure a comfortable podium spot, but a jump into the 20.40s seems unlikely given she hasn't cracked 20.50 m outdoors this season.

**4. Fanny Roos (SWE) – 19.32 m**
The 30-year-old Swede is the clear "best of the rest." Roos has been remarkably consistent in 2026, placing 4th in Shaoxing (19.26 m) and 4th in Stockholm (18.90 m). She is a tough, experienced competitor who rarely has a bad day. While she doesn't have the raw power to challenge the top three, she has a strong technical base and will be highly motivated competing in Scandinavia. Her national record of 19.66 m shows her ceiling, but she hasn't hit that mark consistently this season. Expect a solid, professional performance around 19.30 m to hold off the German and Jamaican challengers.

**5. Yemisi Mabry (GER) – 19.01 m**
The Olympic champion from Paris 2024 has had a strangely subdued 2026 outdoor season. While she looked fearsome indoors—winning the German title with 20.37 m—her outdoor Diamond League form has been shaky. She placed 8th in Shaoxing (18.55 m) and 5th in Stockholm (18.79 m). This inconsistency is a major concern. At 27, she has the talent to challenge for a podium spot, but she hasn't put a full series together outdoors this year. Oslo represents a chance for a reset. If she can find her indoor rhythm, she could leapfrog Roos, but based on recent data, a #5 finish around 19.00 m is the most realistic prediction.

**6. Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM) – 18.84 m**
The veteran Jamaican, now 33, is still a very tough out. She is a former World Indoor silver medalist and has been hovering around the 19-meter mark all season (5th in Shaoxing with 19.12 m, 6th in Stockholm with 18.56 m). She is reliable and gritty, but her peak is likely behind her. She doesn't have the explosive speed to challenge the new generation of throwers. She should land in the 18.80–19.00 m range, which is solid but not enough to trouble the top four or five.

She failed to make the final at the 2025 World Championships (13th in qualifying). Her consistency has deserted her, and she appears to be in a rebuilding phase. Oslo will be a tough ask against this caliber of field.

Her 7th place in Shaoxing (18.79 m) was decent, but a 9th-place finish in Stockholm (17.80 m) was a step back. She is the youngest in the field and has massive potential, but she is still learning how to string together consistent results on the demanding Diamond League circuit. A finish near the bottom is expected, but she will gain invaluable experience.

### Reasoning and Analysis  

#### Top Contenders: Thea Lafond vs. Leyanis Pérez vs. Davisleydi Velazco  
**Thea Lafond** enters Oslo on a crest of outstanding form. At age 31, the Olympic and 2024 World Indoor champion has shown remarkable consistency in 2026: a wind-legal **14.84 m (−1.2)** at the Coqui Cup (17 May) and a **14.73 m (+0.1)** at Lucca just three days before this meeting. Her ability to deliver under pressure (silver at 2025 Worlds with **14.89 m**) and her recent string of 14.70+ legal jumps make her the most reliable candidate for victory. She has also proven she can win at the Bislett Stadion—she placed 5th here in 2025 but with a modest 14.26 m; this season she is a different jumper.  

**Leyanis Pérez** is the reigning World Champion (outdoor and indoor) and still only 23. However, her 2026 outdoor campaign has been quieter than her dominant indoor season (World Indoor gold with **14.95 m**). Her most recent outing, the Znamensky Memorial on 5 June, produced **14.59 m (−0.1)**—a solid but not spectacular mark. Pérez tends to peak for major championships later in the summer, but her raw talent and competitive DNA mean she cannot be counted out. She won the 2025 Oslo Diamond League with **14.72 m** and will be chasing a repeat. Still, Lafond’s higher recent peaks and consistent 14.80-level jumps give her a slight edge.  

**Davisleydi Velazco** (26) has been the revelation of the 2026 outdoor season. She has racked up a series of elite marks: **14.85 m (0.0)** at the Coqui Cup, **14.83 m (−0.2)** at Forbach, **14.71 m (+1.2)** at Filothei, and **14.64 m** in Tenerife. This consistency places her firmly in the 14.70–14.85 range. She also impressed in 2025 with **14.72 m** in Brussels and **14.65 m** in Zürich. Velazco is technically sound and appears to be peaking at exactly the right time. She could challenge for the win, but the experience and big-meet pedigree of Lafond and Pérez may edge her to third.  

#### Middle of the Pack: Saly Sarr, Liadagmis Povea, and Maja Åskag  
**Saly Sarr** (23) has progressed steadily. Her bronze at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (**14.70 m**) announced her arrival on the global stage. Outdoors, she won the African Championships with a wind-aided **14.79 m** and posted **14.57 m** (−0.6) at the Znamensky Memorial. While her legal best outdoors is still below 14.70, she has the momentum and youth to threaten the Cuban trio. A 14.62 m leap is a realistic improvement, placing her fourth.  

**Liadagmis Povea** (29) has struggled for consistency in 2026. After a modest indoor season (4th at Worlds with **14.41 m**), her outdoor marks have been underwhelming: **14.31 m** at the Cuban Championships and **14.19 m** (−0.3) at Znamensky. This is a far cry from her 2025 form when she leaped **14.84 m** in Brescia and **14.72 m** in Zürich. She may find a slight rebound in Oslo, but she appears to be a step behind the top three.  

**Maja Åskag** (23) is a dual-event jumper whose primary focus remains the long jump. Her triple jump in 2026 has been sporadic: a **14.24 m (+0.7)** at Filothei (3 June) is her best outdoor mark of the season—a promising sign. However, she has not broken 14.30 outdoors since 2025, and her indoor season included a poor 12.77 m in Dortmund. She is capable, but Oslo’s elite field will likely push her into the mid-14.20s.  

#### Bottom of the Field: Ackelia Smith and Ivana Španović  
**Ackelia Smith** (23) has not contested a triple jump since the 2025 season, where her best was **14.44 m** at the Jamaican Championships. In 2026, she has competed exclusively in the long jump, with only moderate success (best legal 6.81 m). Without recent triple jump competition, she is a major unknown and is unlikely to challenge the specialists. A **14.10 m** return would be a respectable effort.  

**Ivana Španović** (35) is a long jump legend dabbling in the triple jump. Her 2026 triple jump results are weak: a wind-legal **13.79 m** (−2.4) in Košice and a best indoor mark of **14.41 m** in January. At her age, she cannot match the depth of field here. Her focus is likely on the long jump later in the season, making a sub-14 m performance probable.  

### Conclusion  
The Oslo Diamond League triple jump shapes up as a three-way battle between Lafond, Pérez, and Velazco, with Lafond’s peak form and big-meet mentality giving her a razor-thin advantage. Sarr and Povea will fight for fourth, while Åskag, Smith, and Španović round out the order. The predicted marks reflect the athletes’ recent trajectories and the competitive pressure of a Diamond League setting.
