## Race Preview and Reasoning

### The top three: Ajayi, Seville and Eseme separate themselves

This is a genuinely loaded field, but the strongest case belongs to **Kayinsola Ajayi**. Still only 21, he won the NCAA 100m title in 2026, then produced two massive legal Diamond League wins: **9.84 (+0.1) at the Prefontaine Classic** and **9.84 (-0.7) in London**. In London he beat **Oblique Seville** head-to-head, as he had done earlier in Eugene. That head-to-head record is crucial — Ajayi has now repeatedly out-kicked the reigning world champion in big professional races. His only minor blip was the Commonwealth Games final, where he ran 9.90 and took bronze, but that came after a very fast London race and a long NCAA season. With rest and a Diamond League stage, he is the most logical winner.

**Oblique Seville** is the safest pick for second. The 2025 world champion has the fastest legal time in the field this season: **9.82 (+0.6)** at the Jamaican Championships. He also won Monaco in 9.88 and ran 9.87 in London behind Ajayi. Seville is not as consistently explosive out of the blocks as Ajayi, but his top-end speed is elite. If Ajayi falters even slightly, Seville is the most likely successor.

**Emmanuel Eseme** gets third over the American cluster. At 32, he produced a season-defining win at the Commonwealth Games: **9.83 (+1.3)** in the final, with a 9.89 semi-final. That is better than anything Ronnie Baker or Kenneth Bednarek have done legally in 2026. Eseme’s London race was poor by comparison — only 9.97 — but he has now shown he can follow a bad race with a massive championship-level performance. On the Silesia track, where late-season sprinting can be quick, Eseme should be right in the medals mix.

### The American chase pack: Baker, Bednarek, Anthony, Coleman

Behind the top three, the American contingent is deep but slightly below the top trio.

**Ronnie Baker** has revived his career impressively at 32. At the 2026 US Championships he finished second in the final in **9.88 (+0.8)**, beating both Bednarek and Coleman directly. That head-to-head result gives him the edge here. His start is world-class, and at his best he can challenge 9.85. The question is whether he can produce another 9.87-level run after a long season.

**Kenneth Bednarek** is the most physically powerful sprinter in the field, and his **9.72w (+2.4)** in Los Angeles was the rawest speed anyone has shown this year. But his legal 100m results are less overwhelming: 9.88 at US Champs, 9.96 at Pre, 9.98 in Shaoxing. He is a better 200m runner, and although he finishes strongly, his 100m acceleration still costs him against pure 100m specialists. Fifth is about right, though a shock podium is not impossible if the race comes down to the final 30m.

**Jordan Anthony** is the reigning world indoor 60m champion and has elite top speed — his 6.41 indoor run is the fastest anyone has run this year. Outdoors, he has been excellent but not yet dominant: **9.92 in Monaco** and 9.99 in London. He is still only 21, and his trajectory is clearly upward, but he has not quite shown he can produce 9.85 in a stacked outdoor Diamond League race. Sixth feels fair, with room to move up.

**Christian Coleman** is the toughest former star to rank. The 2019 world champion and 60m world-record holder still has a great start, but his 2026 legal 100m best is only **9.93 (+0.8)** from US Champs, where he finished fourth behind Baker and Bednarek. Coleman’s 9.84w at the LA Grand Prix showed he still has fast legs, but he is no longer consistently breaking 9.90 in legal conditions. At 29, he remains dangerous, but the data says he is now a 9.90–9.95 sprinter rather than a 9.80 sprinter.

### Kennedy, Leotlela and the inconsistent veterans

**Lachlan Kennedy** is the most intriguing outside threat. The 22-year-old Australian won Commonwealth silver with **9.85 (+1.3)**, which is elite-level confirmation of his 60m speed. However, his Diamond League form outside that one race has been moderate: 10.01 in Shaoxing, 10.06 in Xiamen, 10.09 at Pre. If he catches a perfect race, he could challenge for the podium, but his consistency is not yet at Ajayi or Seville’s level.

**Gift Leotlela** has had a quietly good year: he won the 100m in Shaoxing with 9.97, placed second in Xiamen with 10.00, and ran 9.91 at the Commonwealth Games. At 27, he is in his prime, but he lacks the very top-end speed to beat the very best in a fast Diamond League final. Ninth is a fair projection.

**Trayvon Bromell** is the hardest to judge. On pure talent and history, he should be higher. He won the Paris Diamond League in June with **9.91 (+0.1)** and has a 9.85w from Texas. But after Paris, he essentially disappears from the competitive record — no US Championships, no Commonwealth Games, no late-season races. That suggests either injury or a carefully managed training block. At the Silesia meeting in 2025 he was only fifth in 9.97. If he is fit and race-sharp, he could finish top five; if he is rusty, he could fall even further. Tenth is a cautious but data-driven call.

**Romell Glave** became European champion in 2026 with a 10.09 wind-legal win, but his best 100m this summer is a legal **9.97 in London**. That is very good but not enough to crack the top seven here. He is a strong championship runner, but the Diamond League field is deeper than the European Championships field.

### The rest: Blake, Ansah, Simbine, Azu, Blaskowski, de Grasse, Kopeć

**Ackeem Blake** has the talent to be top five, but he has been alarmingly inconsistent in 2026. He ran 9.94 at Jamaican Championships, but then produced 10.06 at Pre, 10.04 in Budapest, and a bizarre 11.55 at the LA Track Festival. At 23, he should be more reliable, but he is not.

**Owen Ansah** is a genuine breakthrough sprinter — the first German under 10 seconds — and his 200m gold at the 2026 European Championships shows he is in great form. But in the 100m, his legal best this season is only 10.00, with a 10.01 in Monaco. He lacks the raw speed of the elite 100m men, though he could run a late-season 9.9x.

**Akani Simbine** remains a class act, and his **9.97 in Paris** shows he can still run fast at 32. But the former African record holder is no longer the consistent 9.85-level threat he was in his prime. He has finished behind the new generation repeatedly, and 14th reflects his current standing.

**Jeremiah Azu** is a proven championship sprinter — European indoor and world indoor 60m champion — but his 100m outdoors has not reached the same level. He ran 10.03 at the Commonwealth Games and 10.16 in the European final. He is competitive, but not quite a sub-9.90 contender.

**Sam Blaskowski** is fascinating because of his 9.89 (+1.5) at the Music City Track Carnival, which suggests genuine 9.85 potential. But his Diamond League results have been far less impressive: 10.06 in Monaco and 10.12 in Budapest. Until he shows he can produce that speed on the big circuit, he remains an outsider.

**Andre de Grasse** is a seven-time Olympic medallist and one of the greatest championship sprinters of his generation, but in 2026 the 100m is clearly his secondary event. He ran 9.95 in Botswana and 10.02 in Paris, but his 200m (19.95) is stronger. At 31, he can still pop a 9.9x on the right day, but a top-five finish here looks beyond him.

**Dominik Kopeć** is a solid European-level sprinter, but his 10.29 at the European final and his Polish title in 10.24 show he is not at the global elite level. In this company, he is the clear outsider.

He also beat Patterson at the US Championships? No, he won USAs in 44.39. So Bailey is clearly elite, but just a step behind the top four on current form.

**Jakob Ingebrigtsen** is second, but not first, because the recent data is not as kind as his reputation. He then won the European 5000m title in 2026, and he remains the most talented runner in the world, but he has no outdoor 1500m result in 2026 to compare with Koech or Wightman. I still expect him to be right there off his class, range, and indoor 3:29.63 form from 2025.

**Jake Wightman** is third. His 3:29.95 in Paris in June 2026 is the single best outdoor 1500m time any of these men has produced this summer. He was also the 2025 world silver medallist and has proven he can deliver in big races. At 31, he may not have the same finishing kick as Koech, but his consistency makes him a clear podium threat. His Euro 6th in a tactical 3:37 race is not a concern for a fast Silesia-style affair.

I think he rebounds in a cleanly paced Diamond League race, but I can’t put him above Wightman given Wightman’s better 2026 1500m clocking and more consistent championship form.

Cheruiyot has a 3:30.28 in Paris and a 2025 world bronze medal, but his Commonwealth Games mile DNF and 11th-place Prefontaine mile make him slightly more volatile. I give Essayi the edge because Cheruiyot’s risk profile is higher.

**Vincent Ciattei** deserves a top-seven spot. He ran 3:30.90 in Rabat and 3:31.63 in Stockholm, making him one of the most reliable 1500m performers in the field in 2026. He also won the US 5000m title just weeks before this race, so he arrives with strong fitness and confidence.

**Hobbs Kessler** is next. The 2000m world record holder has world-class strength, and his 3:31.76 in Stockholm and 4th-place Prefontaine mile show he is close to the front. He still lacks the proven 3:29-level 1500m result that the top four have, but he is dangerous.

**Cole Hocker** is the hardest athlete to place. He is the Olympic champion and world 5000m champion, which gives him enormous pedigree. But his 2026 outdoor mileage has not translated into a standout 1500m or mile: he was 6th at Prefontaine in 3:47.57 and has no 1500m final to judge. In a fast Silesia race, he could easily finish top three, but based on current data I cannot put him above Kessler or Ciattei.

**Stefan Nillessen** is the European champion and deserves respect, but his Euro title came in a slow 3:35.70 final. His 3:32.45 in Paris suggests he can run faster in a paced race, but he has not yet shown the sharp 3:29-3:30 gear of the leaders.

Silesia should deliver an honest, quick race, and Koech’s blend of 2025 U20 record-breaking brilliance and 2026 Budapest form makes him my pick to hold off the more established names.

### Why this order?

**1. Leonardo Fabbri**  
Fabbri is the clear favourite in this field. At 28, he is at peak age, and his 2026 results are the strongest of anyone here. He won the European title in Birmingham with 22.31 m, backed that up with 22.08 m at the Silesia Memorial just four days before this race, and owns the best 2026 outdoor mark in the field with his 22.74 m win at the Prefontaine Classic. He has multiple 22-metre competitions this summer and has beaten most of this Zurich field head-to-head. His 21.47 m in Zurich in 2025 looks like an outlier compared to his 2026 consistency.

**2. Jordan Geist**  
Geist has become the most consistent American this season. He won the US outdoor title with 22.32 m, threw 22.44 m in Memphis, 22.24 m at the Iron Wood Classic, and was runner-up to Fabbri at Silesia with 21.96 m. He was also second at the 2026 World Indoor Championships. Compared to Campbell and Kovacs, Geist has fewer poor competitions and has been reliably in the 21.9–22.4 m range since June. That reliability gives him the edge for silver.

**3. Rajindra Campbell**  
Campbell has the highest ceiling outside Fabbri and Geist. He is the Olympic bronze medallist and Jamaican record holder, and his 2026 season includes big wins at Xiamen with 22.34 m and Zagreb with 22.44 m, plus 22.16 m at the Prefontaine Classic. Those are elite-level results. However, he has also thrown 21.04 m in Rabat and 21.61 m at Silesia, so he remains volatile. I still place him on the podium because his peak throws have been better and more frequent than Kovacs’s 2026 output.

**4. Joe Kovacs**  
Kovacs is the most decorated athlete in the field — a two-time world champion, four-time Olympic medallist, and the second-best shot putter in history with 23.23 m. He also won this exact Zurich meeting in 2025 with 22.46 m. But 2026 has been different. His 22.58 m win in Rabat is excellent, but since then he has mostly been stuck at 21.7–21.9 m, with a poor 21.05 m at Prefontaine and only fourth at the US Championships. At 36, he can still peak for a major final, but I don’t think he can out-throw the younger, more consistent form of Fabbri, Geist, and Campbell.

**5. Adrian Piperi**  
Piperi’s 2026 started badly — 20.10 m in Rome and 20.46 m in Los Angeles — but he has clearly been trending upward. He threw 21.70 m at Prefontaine, 21.77 m in Memphis, 21.91 m to finish second at the US Championships, and 21.64 m at Silesia. At 26, he is ascending, and his recent form puts him just ahead of Otterdahl.

**6. Payton Otterdahl**  
Otterdahl had a strong 2025, including 22.35 m at US Championships and 22.07 m in Zurich, but his 2026 has been less convincing. His best outdoor mark this year is only 21.80 m from Silesia, and he had mediocre throws of 20.55 m at Prefontaine and 20.81 m in Budapest. He still has the strength to beat most of the lower group, but he hasn’t shown the 22-metre form needed to crack the top five in this loaded field.

**7. Roger Steen**  
Steen is a very reliable 21.4–21.9 m thrower. He won the 2026 US indoor title, threw 22.07 m indoors in Belgrade, and outdoors has hit 21.93 m at Drake and 21.83 m in Ústí nad Labem. He doesn’t have the same ceiling as the top four, but he has been consistently ahead of Walsh and Enekwechi in most head-to-head meetings this summer. He finished seventh at Silesia with 21.46 m, which seems about right for this race.

**8. Chukwuebuka Enekwechi**  
Enekwechi is the Commonwealth Games champion after beating Walsh in Glasgow, and he has been remarkably consistent in 2026: 21.74 m at Drake, 21.48 m in Budapest, 21.43 m in Ostrava, and a string of 21.3–21.5 m throws. The issue is that he rarely threatens 22 metres outdoors anymore. Against this Zurich field, that consistency gives him a solid mid-pack finish, but not the top five.

**9. Tom Walsh**  
Walsh is a former world champion and Oceanian record holder with 22.90 m, but at 33 he is no longer the 22-metre force he once was. His 2026 outdoor best is only 21.71 m in Madrid, and he could only manage 21.29 m for eighth at Silesia. He did win the World Indoor title in 2026 with 21.82 m, but outdoors he has been stuck in the 21.0–21.7 m range. Enekwechi beat him at the Commonwealth Games, and Steen has generally been ahead of him this summer, so ninth is fair.

**10. Uziel Muñoz**  
Muñoz’s 2025 World Championship silver medal in Tokyo was a massive breakthrough, but his 2026 form has not matched it. His best outdoor throw this year is 21.46 m in Memphis, and he has frequently been in the 20.2–20.9 m range. At 30, he is experienced, but he simply hasn’t shown the consistency to compete with this group in Zurich. He finishes last unless he can recreate his Tokyo magic.

At just 21, she has had a huge breakout year: Commonwealth silver, European silver behind Zapletalová, a 400m flat time of 50.32, and a personal best of 53.33 in the hurdles. That European final was hugely impressive, but she has yet to produce that kind of run against the full American and Jamaican contingent in a stacked Diamond League final. Her momentum could carry her close to Rushell Clayton, but Clayton’s superior season-long consistency and proven 53.0-level speed give her the edge for bronze.

That lack of sharpness and recent competitive rhythm probably leaves her just outside the top four, though a clean race could push her higher.

She is capable of a top-five finish, but she has not shown the sub-53 speed needed to challenge the leading group.

Fatoumata Binta Diallo should take seventh. Her European bronze in 53.55 was excellent, and she is clearly a talented, improving athlete. But her 54.68 in Lausanne after that European Championships shows she can still be inconsistent across back-to-back high-level races. The clear favourite is Audrey Werro. She is the reigning European 800m champion, she is only 21, and she ran 1:53.80 in Paris in 2026 — the third-fastest time in history. She has also beaten Femke Broeders-Bol in every head-to-head this season, including at Paris, the European Championships and Lausanne. Her Lausanne win over Bol was narrow, 1:55.33 to 1:55.41, but Werro still had the superior finishing strength. On a fast Zürich track, with Bol pushing her, Werro can drop back under 1:55 and should hold on for the win.

Femke Broeders-Bol is the obvious runner-up. Since switching fully to the 800m in 2026, she has been remarkably consistent: 1:55.60 in Paris, 1:55.54 for European bronze, and 1:55.41 in Lausanne. Her 400m speed and 400m hurdles pedigree give her a devastating finish, and she has closed most of the gap to Werro. But she hasn’t yet beaten Werro, and in a championship-style race where Werro controls the pace, Bol may again have to settle for second. She should still run well under 1:55, very close to Werro.

Georgia Hunter Bell is a classy 800m runner, but she arrives in Zürich slightly less 800m-sharp than the top two. She won Commonwealth gold over 800m in 2026 and was the 2025 World Championship silver medallist with 1:54.90. However, her best 800m this year is only 1:55.93 from the UK Championships, and her Commonwealth final was a slow, tactical 1:59.51. She has also been prioritising the 1500m, where she became world indoor and European champion. That means she is fit, but maybe not as specifically explosive over two laps as Werro and Bol. A 1:55.7 from her is strong, but not enough to beat the top two.

Saida Tsehaye is the most exciting outsider. She is just 17, but she has improved enormously through 2026. After running 1:57.96 at Oordegem in early August, she stepped up at Lausanne to run 1:56.92, finishing third behind Werro and Bol and ahead of the Swiss pair. That is a serious time for a teenager, and her upward curve suggests she can go faster still. She might not be consistent enough to beat the established stars yet, but she is clearly the best of the non-Bol/Hunter Bell group.

Sarah Billings is a solid, veteran-level 800m runner. She is the Oceanian record holder and a Commonwealth bronze medallist, and she has run 1:57.01 in Paris this year. That gives her a narrow edge over the chasing pack. However, she hasn’t shown the same rapid improvement as Tsehaye, and her Commonwealth final was only 2:00.61, indicating she may struggle in truly fast, aggressive races. Still, in a paced Diamond League race, Billings should produce another 1:57-class performance.

Jessica Hull is the hardest to predict. She is a world-class 1500m and 3000m runner with an Oceanian-record 800m pedigree, and she made the 800m final at the 2025 World Championships. That means her endurance is superb, but her 800m sharpness is questionable. A 1:57.4 prediction assumes she uses her strength to stay in contact, but she lacks the recent specific speed to challenge Billings or Tsehaye.

Eloisa Coiro is an interesting case: her bio says she is a 400m specialist, but she has developed into a reliable international 800m runner. She reached the European 800m final in 2026, ran 1:58.42 in Rabat and 1:58.59 in Ostrava. Her 400m speed gives her a good last 200m, but her 800m base is not quite as strong as Hull’s or Billings’s. She should lead the second Swiss/Italian group.

The two Swiss runners, Veronica Vancardo and Valentina Rosamilia, are closely matched. Vancardo ran 1:58.68 in Lausanne and finished fourth there, directly ahead of Rosamilia, who ran 1:58.93. Vancardo also had a slightly stronger European final, though both finished 7th and 8th behind Coiro. Their order should mirror Lausanne: Vancardo ahead of Rosamilia, both in the 1:58-1:59 range.

Finally, Myrte van der Schoot is a 400m specialist and 4x400m relay gold medallist, but she is out of her depth in a world-class 800m. She has already failed to finish 800m races in Paris and Lausanne in 2026, and her event is clearly the flat 400m. If she completes the race, she would likely be last in around 2:02-2:03; if she pushes hard from the start as a pacemaker-style runner, she might again fade and fail to finish. Sion is the clear favourite. She is the reigning Olympic and World champion, and her 2026 season has been the most consistent of anyone in the field. She has thrown 68–70 metres repeatedly, with a season best of 73.10 m in Oklahoma in April. More importantly, she has beaten almost everyone almost every time they have met this year: she won Xiamen, Rabat, Stockholm, Los Angeles, the Prefontaine Classic, and the US Championships. Her only loss came to Cierra Jackson in London, where Sion still threw 68.39 m. Her most recent result, 67.89 m to win ISTAF Berlin on 30 August, shows she is still in strong form heading into Brussels.

**2. Jorinde van Klinken**  
Van Klinken has been the most consistent challenger to Sion. She has finished behind Sion in every direct meeting this season, but she has regularly been the next best thrower. Her 70.99 m in Oklahoma was a Dutch record and just 2.11 m behind Sion’s 73.10 m. Since then she has been remarkably reliable: 66.57 m in Stockholm, 67.99 m in London, 67.67 m to win the European Championships, and 66.86 m to win Bellinzona. She has also beaten Cierra Jackson in most of their 2026 meetings, including by nearly four metres in Oklahoma and by 1.45 metres at Bellinzona. That consistency makes her the strong silver-medal pick.

**3. Cierra Jackson**  
Jackson has the single best performance of the season — her 71.72 m Diamond League record in London was outstanding and shows she can beat anyone on the right day. But that result is the clear outlier in her 2026 season. Away from London she has been uneven: 52.90 m in Stockholm, a no-mark at the Prefontaine Classic, 63.22 m in Los Angeles, 67.40 m at US Championships, and 65.41 m at Bellinzona. She is a serious podium threat because of her huge ceiling, but her reliability is not yet at the level of Sion or van Klinken. A bronze medal with a 66–67 m throw feels right.

**4. Shanice Craft**  
Craft has quietly had a strong late-season push. She threw 66.18 m to win the German Championships in July, then took silver at the European Championships with 65.72 m, finishing ahead of Vanessa Kamga. She also has a 66.03 m mark from May. Her early-season Diamond League results were more modest, but her form has improved since mid-summer. In Brussels, she looks more likely to beat Feng and Kamga than the top three.

**5. Bin Feng**  
Feng is a former world champion and Olympic silver medallist, but her 2026 form has been below her peak. She threw 65.03 m at Xiamen and 64.51 m at Rabat, which placed her comfortably ahead of Craft and Kamga in those meets. However, her late-season results dropped off: she only managed 62.51 m at the Chinese Championships in mid-August. She is capable of a 64–65 m throw, but she has not shown the 66–67 m level that would challenge the top three. She likely finishes fifth.

**6. Vanessa Kamga**  
Kamga has talent and a national record of 66.61 m from the 2025 World Championships, plus a European bronze in 2026. But her 2026 season has been inconsistent. She threw 65.30 m in London, but also 59.78 m in Rabat and just 61.93 m in Stockholm. Her most recent result — 62.87 m in Gothenburg on 24 August — was not the kind of momentum a thrower wants going into a Diamond League final. She could easily outperform this prediction if she finds her best, but on the evidence, she is the weakest link in this particular field.

Brussels is the Diamond League final; I expect him to be locked in, win cleanly at 6.20, then take one celebratory record-height attempt after clearing 6.30.

**Karalis** is clearly the No. 2 in this field. His bio notes he is the only other man alongside Duplantis to have cleared 6.20, and his 2026 results are a constant string of runner-up finishes to Duplantis: 6.05 at the World Indoor, 6.00 at the European final, 6.16 in Lausanne, 6.00 in Silesia, and 6.20 in Zurich. He had a shaky spell in the middle of the summer — 5.70 in Shaoxing and 5.62 in Oslo — but he recovered impressively. In Brussels, I see him pushing Duplantis through 6.15 but failing at 6.20.

At 29, he is no longer the 9.76 sprinter he once was, but he still has the start and the competitive reliability to outrun everyone not named Seville or Ajayi.

Leotlela is not explosive enough to challenge the top three, but he is solid, and his 9.92 heat in Silesia showed he can run well even when not in a final.

He can still beat many of the world’s best on a good day, but he lacks the top-end pop to get on the podium in this particular field.

Emmanuel Eseme is the hardest to place. His 9.83 Commonwealth gold was the standout result of his season, and at his best he can beat anyone in this race. But his 9.99 in the Silesia final, where he finished behind Coleman, Leotlela, and Simbine, is a red flag. At 32, his peak performances are becoming more isolated. Gürth’s European bronze and recent 9:15.33 show she is competitive, but her overall ceiling in a fast, high-level Brussels final looks slightly lower than the others.

This is a loaded Brussels Diamond League field, and the rankings should be driven by 2026 form, recent head-to-head results, and each athlete’s proven ceiling.

Ja’Kobe Tharp is the clear favorite. He is the current world-record holder at 20 years old, with his 12.75 from the 2026 NCAA Outdoor Championships standing as the defining performance of the season. His 2026 résumé is remarkable: he beat the majority of this exact field at Budapest with 12.85, won London in 12.89, and claimed Silesia in 13.05. The one blemish, an 8th-place 14.38 in Lausanne, looks like an anomaly rather than a trend, especially because he bounced back to win Silesia and Bellinzona. Tharp has the best speed, the best recent consistency, and the highest ceiling in the race.

Jamal Britt is the strongest challenger. His 12.86 win at the Prefontaine Classic was the best non-Tharp performance of the year, and he also ran 12.89 in Paris and 12.98 in Zagreb. He beat Tharp head-to-head at Prefontaine, which is more than anyone else in this field can say this season. However, Britt has also thrown in some puzzling races, including a 9th-place 26.75 in Rome and a 8th-place 13.85 in Doha. Those inconsistencies, plus narrow losses to Cunningham at London and Silesia, keep him just behind Tharp. Still, his peak speed and multiple sub-13 performances make him the most credible runner-up.

Trey Cunningham is the safest podium pick. The 2022 World Championship silver medalist has been remarkably consistent in 2026: 12.98 in Rome, 13.03 in Los Angeles, 13.07 in Paris, 13.08 in Silesia, and 13.12 in London. He does not have Britt’s flashy 12.86, but he also does not have Britt’s blow-up races. Cunningham beat Britt in both London and Silesia, and his narrow margin in those races suggests he can push for second on a good day. In this prediction, he lands a deserved third because Britt’s superior ceiling outweighs Cunningham’s steadier floor.

Kendry L. Menéndez is the wild card. At just 19, the Cuban has already shown he belongs with the world’s best, running 13.01 in London and 13.02 in Zagreb. In London, he finished ahead of Cunningham, Britt, and Tinch, which is a massive statement for a teenager. His 13.09 in Budapest and 13.14 in Ostrava add further proof that he is a genuine top-four threat. The concern is his DNF in Silesia and his slight drop to 13.20 in Lausanne. That inconsistency is understandable at 19, but it prevents me from putting him on the podium ahead of more seasoned Americans. Still, he is the most dangerous athlete outside the top three.

Cordell Tinch is the reigning world champion and the 2026 US champion, but he has not looked like the same dominant force this summer. His 13.00 win at the US Championships showed he can still deliver under pressure, and he ran 13.06 in Budapest, 13.07 at Prefontaine, and 13.10 in Shaoxing. However, his late-season form has slipped: 13.17 in both Zagreb and London, 13.22 in Silesia, and 13.25 in Brescia. Tinch also competed in the long jump at the US Championships, placing third, which suggests divided focus. Against this world-class field, that leaves him a step behind the top four.

Rachid Muratake has the credentials and early-season speed to be higher, but his 2026 arc has flattened. The Japanese record-holder ran an excellent 13.05 in Osaka and backed it up with 13.13 in Xiamen, but he faded to 13.21 in Paris and 13.41 in Silesia. He also finished behind Bennett at Silesia and behind most of the American contingent whenever they shared the track. Muratake’s ceiling is clearly top-five, but his recent trend makes sixth the safer projection.

Orlando Bennett is a tough one to place. He was the World Championship silver medalist in 2025 and has genuine sub-13 talent. But in 2026 he has been stuck in the 13.15–13.38 range, with his best showing a 13.15 at Prefontaine. He has been consistently competitive but rarely threatening to beat the top Americans this season. His 13.20 at Shaoxing and 13.20 at Xiamen are solid, yet he was behind Muratake in both of those races. That gives Muratake the edge, and leaves Bennett down in seventh.

Elie Bacari rounds out the field. The Belgian has had a solid season, highlighted by a 13.25 national title and a 13.31 fourth-place finish in Bellinzona. He is a proven European-level hurdler and made the 2025 World Championships, but he simply does not have the same firepower as the international medalists in this lineup. His 13.53 in Lausanne and 13.42 in Madrid show he is a step below the sub-13.10 group. A 13.37 in Brussels would be a respectable, honest performance against an elite field, but it should leave him last.

His only issue is that he has not quite had the late-season edge over Hocker or Koech in direct 1500m meetings. Still, with his 2024 Olympic bronze and 3:27.80 PB, he is the clear third pick.

**Putting Ingebrigtsen fifth feels drastic, but the recent evidence is hard to ignore.** In 2025, Ingebrigtsen was shockingly eliminated early in the World Championship 1500m and then finished 10th in the 5000m final. In 2026, he won the European 5000m title, but in his two late-season 1500m Diamond League appearances he was fourth in Silesia and fifth in Zürich, behind Hocker, Koech, and Nuguse both times. He remains world-class, but his 1500m sharpness is not currently matching his 5000m strength.

But he followed it with 10th place in Zürich in 3:32.95. That sort of swing makes him dangerous but unreliable, so sixth is a fair middle ground.

**Cheruiyot is still a factor, but no longer a podium certainty.** He ran 3:30.67 in Stockholm and won the Oslo Mile, but he faded to 11th in Zürich. At 30, he can still beat most of the field on a good day, but the younger Americans and Koech have clearly moved past him in head-to-head matchups.

Farken is in strong form and was second in Berlin, but his Zürich and Stockholm finishes were behind both Ciattei and Kessler. Heyward had a good sixth in Silesia but dropped to ninth in Zürich. Javelin Throw Women.blurb:
**Predicted results — Women’s Javelin Throw, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**

### Why this order?

**Ziyi Yan** is the clear favourite. At 17, she has already produced the best throw in the world this season by a wide margin: 71.74 m at Xiamen, a world U20 record and Asian record and the second-best mark in history. Even her “quieter” Diamond League wins this season — 67.11 m in Oslo, 67.44 m in Paris, 68.75 m in Monaco — are better than anything the rest of this field has produced in 2026. She is the most consistent, the most powerful, and the most obvious winner. I expect her to win comfortably, though perhaps not matching her 71.74 m again in a final setting.

**Haruka Kitaguchi** gets second because of her late-season peak. The reigning Olympic champion was poor in the middle of the season: 60.08 m in Xiamen and only 56.24 m in Monaco. But she turned things around dramatically with a 64.90 m win in Lausanne on 21 August, beating both Ruiz Hurtado and Vilagoš head-to-head. That result, plus her proven championship pedigree, gives her the edge for second.

**Flor Denis Ruiz Hurtado** is the biggest threat to Kitaguchi. Her 67.34 m at the CAC Games in early August is outstanding and shows she can still produce a huge throw at 34. But she also had a no-mark in Monaco and a string of 60–61 m Diamond League results before that. She followed her 67.34 m with 64.29 m in Lausanne — excellent, but behind Kitaguchi. I place her third: dangerous, but slightly less reliable than Kitaguchi at the sharp end.

**Adriana Vilagoš** is the clear fourth. She has a big personal ceiling from 2025 — including 67.22 m — but her 2026 season has mostly been in the 59–63 m range. She did win European bronze with 60.93 m and then threw 62.28 m in Lausanne, which is solid. Still, she has not shown the same firepower as Kitaguchi or Ruiz Hurtado this season, and she was behind both in Lausanne. She should be comfortably ahead of the bottom two, though.

**Sigrid Borge** takes fifth, despite a disappointing late season. Her 65.00 m at Xiamen in May was a major standout, and she also threw 61.92 m in Oslo. But after that she faded badly: 56.92 m in Paris, 56.57 m in Monaco, and 54.51 m at the Norwegian Championships. She recovered a bit with 59.98 m in the European final, which is why I still have her ahead of Sietiņa. Her ceiling is higher than anything Sietiņa has shown in 2026, even if she has been inconsistent.

**Anete Sietiņa** is sixth. She has the best championship credential in this group after Kitaguchi — a silver medal at the 2025 World Championships with 64.64 m. But her 2026 form has not matched that level at all. Her best this season is only 60.05 m, she had a no-mark in Paris, and she failed to make the European final after throwing 56.24 m in qualifying. She did beat Borge narrowly at Lausanne, 58.73 m to 58.54 m, but over the full season Borge has shown a higher peak and a better recent championship performance. I give Borge the nod for fifth, with Sietiņa sixth.

Shot Put Men.blurb:
Predicted finish – Men’s Shot Put, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Jordan Geist (USA) – 22.63 m  
2. Rajindra Campbell (JAM) – 22.47 m  
3. Leonardo Fabbri (ITA) – 22.35 m  
4. Joe Kovacs (USA) – 21.82 m  
5. Tom Walsh (NZL) – 21.54 m  
6. Roger Steen (USA) – 21.30 m  

---

**Reasoning:**

This is a deep field, but the most compelling form lines point to a Jordan Geist victory. At 27, Geist is in the prime stretch of his career and has been the most consistent shot putter in the world through the late 2026 season. He arrives in Brussels off a Diamond League win in Zürich with 22.53 m, where he beat Campbell, Fabbri, Kovacs, Steen, and Walsh in the same kind of head-to-head field he’ll see again. Geist also won the US outdoor title with 22.32 m, threw 22.44 m in Memphis, and was consistently above 21.9 m in his final pre-Brussels series. His floor is remarkably high — even his “off” Diamond League meetings in Xiamen and Rabat were 21.52 m and 21.56 m. With the Diamond League final on the line, Geist should be trusted to produce a slight season’s best around 22.6 m.

**Rajindra Campbell** is the biggest threat. The 29-year-old Jamaican Olympic bronze medallist and national record holder has serious late-season momentum, including a 22.59 m victory in Brescia on 30 August and a 22.22 m runner-up effort in Zürich. He has also won Xiamen with 22.34 m and Zagreb with 22.44 m. But Campbell’s pattern is more volatile than Geist’s: he threw only 21.04 m in Rabat, 21.39 m in Rome, and 21.61 m in Silesia. He can absolutely win if he catches one, but Geist has been better at producing big throws when the stakes are highest. Campbell should finish just behind, around 22.47 m.

**Leonardo Fabbri** is still the most credentialed European in the field. At 28, the two-time European champion and 2026 European gold medallist has had a brilliant season. His 22.74 m victory at the Prefontaine Classic in July is the best outdoor mark any of these six athletes has managed in 2026. He has also been extremely reliable: Italian champion with 22.43 m, European champion with 22.31 m, and a consistent run of 22.0–22.2 m late in the season. However, he was third in Zürich behind Geist and Campbell, and second behind Campbell in Brescia. In a final where the top two are peaking, Fabbri might need a perfect series to jump ahead. He should still medal with 22.35 m.

**Joe Kovacs** is the veteran wildcard. At 36, he remains one of the greatest shot putters ever — second on the all-time list with 23.23 m, with multiple world titles and Olympic silvers. But the 2026 season shows his consistency has slipped. He did win Rabat with a superb 22.58 m, but he was eighth at the Prefontaine Classic, fourth at the US Championships, fourth in Zürich, and fifth in Brescia. He still has the power to beat nearly anyone on a given day, but at this age and with this recent form, it is hard to place him above three younger throwers who are throwing 22.2 m or better more regularly. Expect a solid but not spectacular 21.82 m and fourth.

**Tom Walsh** should finish fifth. The 33-year-old New Zealander is a former world champion, Olympic bronze medallist, and the Oceanian record holder with 22.90 m. He also won the 2026 World Indoor title with 21.82 m and took Commonwealth silver in Glasgow. But his outdoor form in 2026 has been stuck in the 21.1–21.7 m range. He was seventh at Prefontaine, eighth in Silesia, and sixth in Zürich. Walsh is competitive but no longer has the pop to challenge the 22.5 m-level throwers outdoors. A 21.54 m mark would be a fair representation of his current level.

**Roger Steen** rounds out the field. The 33-year-old American is a two-time World Indoor medallist and the reigning US indoor champion, but his late 2026 outdoor campaign has faded badly. After a strong indoor season and a 21.93 m Drake Relays win, he had no-mark and 19.81 m efforts at the Ed Murphey Classic, then only 21.06 m at US Championships, 21.46 m in Silesia, and 21.53 m in Zürich. In a field like this, Steen is likely to be chasing the others from the first round. Sixth place with 21.30 m seems the most probable outcome.

Ultimately, this final should come down to Geist and Campbell. Geist gets the edge because he has been sharper in head-to-head competition, more stable across the entire season, and is peaking at exactly the right time for the Diamond League final.

Triple Jump Men.blurb:
**Predicted finish – Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:**

1. **Andy Díaz Hernández (ITA)** – **18.03 m**  
2. **Pedro Pichardo (POR)** – **17.86 m**  
3. **Yasser Mohammed Triki (ALG)** – **17.72 m**  
4. **Jordan Scott (JAM)** – **17.49 m**  
5. **Lázaro Martínez (CUB)** – **17.21 m**  
6. **Almir dos Santos (BRA)** – **16.98 m**

---

**Why this order?**

This is a very strong field, but the form lines going into Brussels are uneven. Some athletes are peaking, some are fading, and some have been brilliant in lower-level meetings but unable to transfer that to the Diamond League circuit. My prediction is based on 2026 results, head-to-head meetings, and the trajectory of each athlete since the major championships.

**1. Andy Díaz Hernández** – After a wobble at Lausanne, Andy remains the man to beat. His European Championships victory in August was the defining outdoor performance of the year: **18.15 m (+1.7)** is the biggest legal mark on the board for this entire group. He also won the World Indoor title in March with 17.47 m, won in Roma with 17.59 m, repeated 17.59 m in Oslo, and produced 17.87 m to win the Italian title. The only real blemish was a modest 17.20 m at Lausanne, where he finished third behind Pichardo and Triki. That looks like a post-Euro flat spot. At 30 and with his recent championship pedigree, he is the most likely jumper in a loaded final to produce something close to 18 metres. I expect him to bounce back with an 18.03 m winner.

**2. Pedro Pichardo** – The reigning world champion and 2020 Olympic gold medallist is the biggest threat. Pichardo has been remarkably solid in 2026: 17.71 m in Doha, 17.76 m at the European Championships in Birmingham, and a 17.44 m win at Lausanne into a **-1.0 m/s** headwind, which is excellent raw jumping. He also beat Díaz head-to-head in Lausanne, and he has the pedigree to win any final. However, he has not matched Andy’s ceiling this season — Andy beat him convincingly at the European final, 18.15 m to 17.76 m. Pichardo is the safer pick for consistency, but I think Andy still has the higher peak, and Brussels should be a peak performance. Pichardo lands in the low 17.80s, close but second.

**3. Yasser Mohammed Triki** – Triki has been the quietest consistent performer in the world this summer. He has produced a string of high-quality marks: **17.67 m** in Doha, **17.58 m** in Linz, **17.47 m** legal in Madrid, **17.35 m** indoors in Liévin, and a World Indoor bronze. At Lausanne he again finished second, with a wind-assisted 17.43 m, and his legal 17.21 m was still competitive with Andy’s 17.20 m. Triki does not yet have the 18-metre threat of Díaz or Pichardo, but he very rarely has a bad competition. That reliability should lift him to third ahead of Jordan Scott, especially given Scott’s late-season inconsistency.

**4. Jordan Scott** – Scott’s best is right there with the top three. His **17.69 m** in Doha and **17.66 m** in Caguas are serious marks, and he has a World Indoor silver medal and Commonwealth gold in 2026. But his season has been jagged: in Oslo his 17.66 m was wind-assisted and his legal mark was only 16.96 m; he no-marked at Memphis in July; and at Lausanne he could only manage **16.86 m**, finishing behind Triki, Díaz, and Pichardo. Scott has the talent to beat Triki on a good day, but Belgium is late in the season and his form has trended downward since Doha. I have him fourth, still capable of 17.49 m, but not quite consistent enough to hold off Triki.

**5. Lázaro Martínez** – Martínez has a World Championship bronze medal from 2025 and a solid 17.33 m in Oslo in 2026, so the talent is real. But his inconsistency is glaring. He had a disastrous no-contest indoors at the 2025 World Indoor Championships, managed only 15.42 m in Doha in June, and was a subdued sixth at Lausanne with 16.69 m. He did win the CAC Games, but the level there was not comparable to Brussels. In a field this strong, he is more likely to be fighting for fifth/sixth than for the podium. I predict a 17.21 m rebound, but it will not be enough to crack the top four.

**6. Almir dos Santos** – Almir is the oldest of the group at 32 and perhaps the hardest to read. He won the Pan American title with 17.24 m and the Brazilian title with 17.07 m, so he can still jump well in the right setting. But his Diamond League results in 2026 have been poor: 16.22 m in Roma, 15.85 m at Oslo, and 16.20 m at Lausanne. Against this particular field, those marks put him firmly in last. The step up in competition seems to expose technical issues or an inability to get into rhythm in high-pressure DL finals. He could still produce something respectable, but 16.98 m feels like a fair projection, and I don’t see him overtaking any of the five ahead of him.

400m Women.blurb:
**Predicted finish – Women’s 400m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**

1. **Marileidy Paulino** (DOM) – **48.61**  
2. **Henriette Jæger** (NOR) – **49.12**  
3. **Nickisha Pryce** (JAM) – **49.25**

7. **Roxana Gómez** (CUB) – **50.18**  
8. **Helena Ponette** (BEL) – **50.62**

---

### Why this order?

**Marileidy Paulino is the clear No. 1.**  
Paulino is the Olympic champion, the world No. 1, and has been the most dominant woman in the event for years. Her 2026 season is a string of sub-49 performances: **48.48 in Paris**, **48.67 in Monaco**, **48.87 in Silesia**, **48.94 at the CAC Games final**, and **48.97 in London**. No one else in this field can match that consistency or that ceiling. She also ran 47.98 at the 2025 World Championships final, showing a championship gear no one here possesses. The only question in Brussels is not whether she wins, but by how much.

**Henriette Jæger gets the nod for silver, despite a rough Silesia.**  
Jæger’s standout result is her **49.04 European Championship win** in Birmingham in August. That is the fastest 400m of anyone in this race outside Paulino and Aaliyah Butler’s 48.84. More importantly, Jæger has repeatedly beaten Nickisha Pryce head-to-head in 2026: she was ahead of Pryce in Roma, Oslo, and London, including a strong **49.15 to 50.09** win in London. Her seventh-place 49.85 at Silesia is a blip, likely a post-championship flat spot after her European title. If she is anywhere near her 49.04 form, she is the second-best runner in this field.

**Nickisha Pryce is the most dangerous late-season riser.**  
Pryce has been excellent in the closing weeks of the season. Her **49.27 win in Brescia** was her best of 2026, and she followed her **49.49 at Silesia** by beating Jæger, Bukowiecka, Butler, and Gómez there. She may not have Jæger’s championship peak, but she has been more consistent recently. The concern is that in their earlier 2026 meetings, Jæger usually beat her by a clear margin. Pryce has genuine podium potential, and if Jæger repeats her Silesia performance, Pryce could easily take second. But based on overall ceiling and head-to-head form, she settles for third.

**Natalia Bukowiecka is the reliable veteran.**  
Bukowiecka rarely runs badly. The Polish record-holder and Olympic/World medallist delivered **49.57 in the European semi-final** and **49.60 at Silesia**, both strong late-season marks. She has a lower ceiling than Butler or Manuel, but a much higher floor. Her European silver with 50.04 was solid, and she has the experience to execute in a deep Diamond League field. She is the clear fourth pick ahead of the younger, more erratic talents.

**Aaliyah Butler is the wild card, and the toughest ranking decision.**  
Butler’s **48.84 in Monaco** is the fastest anyone has run this season apart from Paulino. It is a genuinely elite mark, and she is the US champion. But she has not reproduced anything close to that since: **49.93 at US Championships** and **50.38 at Silesia**. That is a worrying trend. She could absolutely win or take second if she rediscovers Monaco form, but a prediction should weigh consistency, not just a single brilliant performance. I place her fifth, ahead of Manuel because of her superior peak, but behind Bukowiecka due to reliability.

**Lurdes Gloria Manuel has talent but is hard to trust after her European final.**  
Manuel is the world indoor champion and ran **49.37 in Paris** and **49.44 in Monaco**, so the ability is there. But at the European Championships final, she faded hard to **50.86**, which was a major missed opportunity. She then skipped the 400 at Silesia, running a fast 300m instead. That suggests her 400m rhythm may be off at the back end of the season. I expect her to be competitive and maybe split the difference, but she is not quite as strong a bet as Bukowiecka or the top three.

**Roxana Gómez and Helena Ponette round out the field.**  
Gómez has been a reliable 50-second runner in 2026, with a best of **49.99 at the CAC Games final**, but her Diamond League form has slipped to **50.37, 50.14, and 50.88**. She was a 49.48 runner at the 2025 World Championships, but this year she has not shown enough sustained speed to challenge the top five. Ponette is a solid European-level competitor, with a season’s best of **50.31 in the Euro semi-final**, but her **51.43 in the Euro final** shows she is still a step below the top group. Both are likely fighting for seventh and eighth rather than the podium.

**2. Tina Clayton**  
Clayton is the biggest threat. She already has a World Championships silver medal in the 100m from 2025, when she ran **10.76**, and she has twice run **10.85** in 2026 — at Rabat and the Jamaican Championships. That puts her clearly ahead of everyone except Richardson. However, her post-June form has been more mixed: she was fifth at Prefontaine, sixth in Silesia, and fourth in Zürich, while Richardson was ahead of her in the latter races. At 21, Clayton has enormous upside, but on current form she is the clear second-best in this field rather than a genuine favourite to beat Richardson.

**3. Amy Hunt**  
Hunt is the best of the Europeans by some margin. She won the 100m at the 2026 European Championships in **11.00**, and her legal season’s best of **10.97** from Stockholm shows she can threaten 10.9. She also ran **10.98** to take Commonwealth silver behind Hobbs in July. Since then, she has actually closed the gap on Hobbs, finishing ahead of her in Zürich with **11.04** to Hobbs’s 11.18. Hunt is only 23 but already a proven major-final performer. She has the biggest medal haul of any non-American/Jamaican in this race, and her 2026 arc is still upward.

**4. Zoe Hobbs**  
Hobbs is hard to place because her best is clearly better than her recent results. She became the first New Zealand woman to win a Commonwealth Games 100m title, running **10.93** in Glasgow. That remains the fastest time by any non-Richardson/Clayton athlete in this field this season. But her post-Commonwealth form has faded: **11.05** in Silesia, **11.18** in Zürich, and **11.16** in Bellinzona. I still place her fourth because her 10.93 ceiling is better than the Europeans below her, and she has repeatedly shown she can produce on big stages. If she hits her best, she could even challenge Hunt; if she reproduces her late-August form, she could slip further.

**5. Delphine Nkansa**  
Nkansa is the most improved athlete in this field. She was seventh in the 2025 Worlds relay but has since developed into a genuine European medal threat. At the 2026 European Championships she won 100m bronze in **11.06**, having run **11.09** in the semi-final. She also beat both van der Weken and Dosso in that final, which gives her the head-to-head edge here. Her Belgian title in **11.13** and a consistent run of sub-11.2 races suggest she is in career-best shape. The gap to Hunt is real, but Nkansa is the clear next-best European.

**6. Patrizia van der Weken**  
Van der Weken is extremely consistent but lacks the ceiling of the athletes above her. She ran **11.05** in Stockholm, **11.08** at the European Championships semi-final, and **11.10** in the final. She has a strong start — proven by her 60m medals indoors — but over 100m she tends to hold position rather than accelerate past people. She is a reliable 11.05–11.10 performer, which puts her in the middle of this pack but not on the podium.

**7. Jonielle Smith**  
This is a deliberately harsh ranking, but it is based on form and fitness. Smith ran **10.89** at the Prefontaine Classic in July and looked like a top-four threat. Since then, however, she finished sixth in Budapest, missed the Commonwealth final after reaching the semi-final, and ran only **11.14** in Zürich. Withdrawing from a major final is a major red flag, and her subsequent performances suggest she is either carrying a small injury or has lost her sharpness. On pure season’s best she belongs higher, but in Brussels she cannot be placed above healthy athletes who are consistently running 11.0–11.1.

**8. Zaynab Dosso**  
Dosso is a world-class indoor 60m runner — she is the reigning World Indoor champion over 60m — but her outdoor 100m has not matched that level. Her 2026 legal best is only **11.07**, and she ran **11.12** in the European final before closing with **11.26** in Bellinzona. That poor late-season run drops her below van der Weken and Nkansa. Her start will look great for the first 30 metres, but in this field she does not have the top-end speed to convert it into a high finish.

**9. Boglárka Takács**  
Takács is a national record holder and a strong Hungarian champion, but the data says she is outclassed here. Her legal 100m best in 2026 is only **11.16**. She did run **10.93** at the European Championships, but that was wind-aided, and in the semi-final she ran just **11.13**, which was not enough to reach the final. Her recent results — **11.31** in late August — suggest she is not arriving in Brussels in peak form. In a race this strong, she is the likely last-place finisher.

---

**Final takeaway:** Richardson wins from Clayton, with Hunt leading the European challenge. The most interesting battle is behind them, where Hobbs’s ceiling, Nkansa’s momentum, and van der Weken’s consistency will decide places four through six. Smith is the wild card, but her fitness concerns are too serious to ignore.

Against this field, fifth is his likely ceiling, unless others falter.

**Timothy Herman** is clearly last. At 35, he has been stuck around **72–77 m** all season, failed to make the European final, and has no result remotely close to the rest of the field. His national-record ability is in the past. In a Diamond League final against this level of competition, seventh is the only realistic outcome.

Her 12.53 in Bellinzona just before Brussels suggests she is in good shape, and she should beat Skrzyszowska on recent head-to-head form.

Pia Skrzyszowska started the outdoor season strongly with 12.44 in Nancy and 12.46 in Paris, but she has faded late in the summer: 12.64 in Chorzów and 12.70 in Zürich. She is still a fine hurdler, but at this level, 12.61 would be a decent return to form. She does not appear to have the late-season sharpness to challenge the top six.

Yanla Ndjip-Nyemeck is the youngest and least proven in this company. She has improved into a 12.8-level hurdler, with a Belgian record-equalling season, but she finished seventh in the European final in 12.97 and ran 12.87 in Bellinzona. Brussels will be a step up in quality. A 12.82 would be a strong showing, but she is unlikely to crack the top seven against this elite field.

3000m Steeplechase Men.blurb:
**Predicted finish – Men’s 3000m Steeplechase, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:**

1. **Soufiane el Bakkali (MAR)** – 7:57.79  
2. **Gemechu Godana (ETH)** – 8:00.12  
3. **Simon Koech (KEN)** – 8:01.08  
4. **Salah Eddine ben Yazide (MAR)** – 8:03.36  
5. **Edmund Serem (KEN)** – 8:04.05  
6. **Ruben Querinjean (LUX)** – 8:05.58  
7. **Samuel Firewu (ETH)** – 8:06.43  
8. **Karl Bebendorf (GER)** – 8:08.77  
9. **Ryuji Miura (JPN)** – 8:09.42  
10. **Matthew Wilkinson (USA)** – 8:10.89  
11. **Daniel Arce (ESP)** – 8:11.95  
12. **Rémi Schyns (BEL)** – 8:25.46  
13. **Wilberforce Chemiat Kones (KEN)** – DNF  

---

**Why this order?**

El Bakkali remains the man to beat. His 7:57.25 in Rabat in May was the fastest steeplechase of the season by anyone in this field, and his Diamond League wins in Stockholm and Doha confirm consistency. He did lose to Godana at Silesia in August, but in a high-stakes Brussels final I still trust the two-time Olympic champion and former world champion to respond. Godana’s 8:02.74 win at Silesia, plus his African Championships title, make him the clear second favourite; at 20 he is the most rapidly improving athlete in the race.

Simon Koech gets third because his Rabat 7:59.44 and Monaco 8:03.35 are elite-level marks. He has also beaten Edmund Serem several times, notably in Rabat and Monaco. However, his Stockholm 8:13.40 and Commonwealth Games loss to Serem show he can be vulnerable when the race is more tactical. In an honest, fast Brussels race, his Rabat/Monaco form should resurface.

The 4th-7th group is where the toughest calls sit. Salah Eddine ben Yazide gets 4th because of his excellent Silesia run: 8:05.08 in third, directly ahead of Querinjean and clearly ahead of Serem. He also ran 8:09.88 to win Ostrava, and has been far more consistent through August than Serem. Edmund Serem has the higher ceiling — he ran 8:01.61 in Rabat and won Commonwealth gold — but his post-Rabat form has hovered around 8:08-8:18, and he lost ground to ben Yazide at Silesia. I still place him 5th because of that ceiling and his junior-level pedigree.

Ruben Querinjean is the wildcard. His 8:05.36 at Silesia was a genuine breakthrough, and he has already won a Diamond League meeting in Brussels in 2025. That matters. He gets 6th, just ahead of Samuel Firewu, because Querinjean beat Firewu head-to-head at Silesia. Firewu remains a very strong runner — 4th at the 2025 World Championships and 8:06.65 at Silesia — but he has not quite shown the finishing kick of the men directly above him.

Karl Bebendorf is the best of the next group. His Paris win in 8:05.55 was a standout result, and he also finished ahead of Miura, Wilkinson and Arce at Silesia. Ryuji Miura has the strongest raw talent of the remaining runners — his 8:10.30 in Monaco and Japanese record pedigree show that — but his DNF in Hiroshima and 8:23.97 in Stockholm are red flags. Wilkinson is steady rather than spectacular; Arce is still capable of 8:11 but at 33 is unlikely to outrun the younger, sharper steeplechasers.

Rémi Schyns is outclassed at this level based on his European Championships 8:29.25 and lack of Diamond League pedigree. And Wilberforce Chemiat Kones, once a useful Kenyan steeplechaser, has DNFed so often in 2026 — including in Brussels, Paris, Monaco, Stockholm and Ostrava — that I cannot confidently give him a finishing time. He is predicted to drop out.

800m Women.blurb:
Predicted finish — Brussels Diamond League, Women’s 800m, 4 September 2026:

1. Audrey Werro (SUI) — 1:53.55  
2. Femke Broeders-Bol (NED) — 1:54.32  
3. Saida Tsehaye (ETH) — 1:56.48  
4. Sarah Billings (AUS) — 1:57.62  
5. Addison Wiley (USA) — 1:57.95  
6. Veronica Vancardo (SUI) — 1:58.36  
7. Prudence Sekgodiso (RSA) — 1:58.76  
8. Oratile Nowe (BOT) — 2:00.18  
9. Rachel Klopfenstein (MRI) — 2:00.92  
10. Camille Laus (BEL) — 2:01.45  

---

This is a deep, end-of-season Diamond League 800m, and the hierarchy is fairly clear at the top. **Audrey Werro** is the overwhelming favourite. At just 21, she arrives as the reigning European champion and has been the dominant force all summer: Euro gold in 1:54.81, DL wins in Paris in 1:53.80, Stockholm in 1:53.98, Ostrava in 1:54.45, and that stunning 1:53.70 in Zürich — the third-fastest 800m in history. Nobody in this field can match her raw strength or her ability to run a genuine 1:53-1:54 pace. I expect another fast, controlled front-run from Werro, possibly a small PB improvement.

**Femke Broeders-Bol** is a clear second. The former 400m hurdles world champion has adapted brilliantly to the 800m in 2026. She was right behind Werro in Lausanne (1:55.41) and Zürich (1:54.71), and she took European bronze in 1:55.54. Her background gives her exceptional speed and race poise, but Werro has simply been better every time they’ve met this season. Bol’s 1:54.71 is far ahead of anyone else in this field, so second place looks locked.

The most interesting battle is for third. I’m giving it to 17-year-old **Saida Tsehaye**. She was third in Lausanne in 1:56.92, ahead of Vancardo, Wiley, Sekgodiso and Nowe, and fourth in Zürich in 1:57.33 behind Werro, Bol and likely another non-field athlete. She also set the Ethiopian U20 record this season. Her youth is remarkable, but her 2026 trajectory is real and rapid. She has the best recent credentials of anyone outside the Werro/Bol top two.

For fourth, I’m taking **Sarah Billings**. Her best 800m this year was 1:57.01 in Paris, where she finished just behind Sekgodiso but ahead of Nowe. She also has great range, shown by her 1500m best of 3:56.73 and Commonwealth bronze over 800m. Billings was a bit flat in Zürich (1:59.67) after a quick turnaround from a strong 1500m, but with a week’s recovery she should be sharper. She has the speed and endurance to lead the chase pack behind Tsehaye.

**Addison Wiley** is next. She has been solid without being spectacular at 800m in 2026, running 1:57.98 in Doha and 1:57.70 in Eugene. She is the American record holder at 1000m and won bronze at the World Indoor 800m in Toruń, so she has proven big-race credentials. Her 3:58.96 1500m in Bellinzona at the end of August shows she is still in excellent shape. Her loss to Vancardo at Lausanne is a concern, but her overall ceiling and recent fitness tip her to edge out the more consistent Vancardo in Brussels.

**Veronica Vancardo** is harder to overlook. She has been remarkably consistent: 1:58.49 in Zürich, 1:58.68 in Lausanne, and sub-1:59 in most major races. She beat Wiley head-to-head in Lausanne and beat Billings in Zürich. But her peak speed is slightly lower than Billings or Wiley, and in a fast Diamond League race, that matters. I see her settling into sixth, just outside the 1:58 barrier.

**Prudence Sekgodiso** is the biggest puzzle. She was the 2025 World Indoor champion and ran 1:56.83 in Paris this year, which would put her right in the top four if that version shows up. But her season has fallen apart since: she was poor at the Commonwealth Games, failed to make the final after a 2:01.57 semifinal, and then ran 1:59.58 in Lausanne. Her talent is clear, but her recent form is too unreliable to rank above Vancardo, Wiley or Billings. I’m putting her seventh, though she could easily be fourth if she recaptures her Paris form.

**Oratile Nowe** has a decent season’s best of 1:57.32 from Rabat, but her late-season results have been troubling: 2:00.89 in Lausanne, 2:01.29 in the Commonwealth final and 2:01.08 in Berlin. She is a nationally record-breaking athlete and has run close to the leaders this year, but she appears to be running out of steam. I expect her to struggle to stay with the 1:58 group.

**Rachel Klopfenstein** set the Mauritian record of 1:58.73 in Ostrava, but her 2026 season has also been defined by DNFs and inconsistency. She was eighth in the Commonwealth final in 2:03.81 and did not finish in Bellinzona at the end of August. If she holds together, she could challenge for seventh or eighth, but I can’t trust her to be sharp in a tough DL race. I have her ninth.

**Camille Laus** is a talented Belgian sprinter/relay athlete, but her 800m still reads like a secondary event. She ran 1:59.43 in a European Championship heat, but then finished only seventh in that heat and didn’t progress. Her Belgian Championships 800m final was 2:06.31, and her focus remains largely on the 4x400m relay. In this field, she lacks the sustained 800m credentials of the others, so I place her last.

Ultimately, Werro and Bol separate themselves early, Tsehaye leads the chasing pack, and the middle depends on who is sharpest late in a long season. Brussels should produce a fast, honest race — and Werro should take another Diamond League scalp in what has already been a historic season.

400m Hurdles Men.blurb:
Predicted finish and marks — Men’s 400m Hurdles, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Alison dos Santos (BRA) – 46.21  
2. Matheus Lima (BRA) – 47.18  
3. Ezekiel Nathaniel (NGR) – 47.31  
4. Emil Agyekum (GER) – 47.53  
5. Trevor Bassitt (USA) – 47.69  
6. Caleb Dean (USA) – 47.84  
7. Abderrahman Samba (QAT) – 47.93  
8. Matic Ian Guček (SLO) – 48.06  

### Why this order

**Alison dos Santos is the obvious winner.** He arrives in Brussels as the world-record holder after running 45.80 in Zürich on 27 August. That came on top of a dominant 2026 Diamond League season: 46.72 in Xiamen, 47.11 in Stockholm, 46.89 in Oslo, 46.43 in Silesia, and 46.48 at the Brazilian Championships. Nobody else in this field has shown anything close to that level. Even with a possible post-record letdown, he should still win comfortably in the low-46s.

**Matheus Lima gets 2nd on consistency and late-season PB form.** His 47.26 at Silesia was the best non-Alison time among these athletes in the late season, and he followed it with 47.57 in Zürich. He also ran 47.37 in Stockholm and 47.64 in Ostrava. His August PB, mentioned in his bio, shows he is still improving. He lost to Nathaniel by 0.07 in Zürich, but he beat Nathaniel by 0.57 in Silesia, and his overall rhythm in the 47.2–47.6 range is more reliable.

**Ezekiel Nathaniel is right behind.** The 22-year-old Commonwealth champion has a 47.37 season’s best and ran a sharp 47.50 in Zürich. His flat 400m speed — 45.32 at the Prefontaine Classic — is a big weapon. But his season was a bit more uneven: 48.30 in London and 48.47 in the Commonwealth final show he can still drift off his best. In a fast Brussels race, he should be in the 47.2–47.4 range, but Lima’s extra consistency gives him the nod.

**Emil Agyekum is the best of the next group.** The German record holder and European silver medallist ran 47.45 in London and won Budapest in 47.58, beating several of the same men. However, his most recent results — 47.87 at the European final and 48.18 at ISTAF — suggest he is not quite sharp enough to challenge the 47.2-level men right now. He should still hold off the Americans for 4th.

**Trevor Bassitt has the talent to be higher.** His 47.37 at the USATF Lone Star Grand Prix and 47.59 at Budapest show he can mix with the top challengers. But his 48.71 at Silesia was a real warning sign. In a loaded final, I think he lands just outside the medals in the low-47.7s.

**Caleb Dean is the boom-or-bust pick.** He has real speed: 47.42 at USATF, 47.62 at Budapest, 47.75 in Xiamen. But he also ran 50.45 in London and DNF’d in Silesia. His ceiling is higher than Samba’s, and he beat Samba head-to-head in Budapest (47.62 to 48.31), so I place him 6th. Still, he is the hardest athlete to trust on a week-to-week basis.

**Abderrahman Samba is a faded force.** The 30-year-old former sub-47 star showed a glimpse with 47.77 in Zürich, but that was surrounded by 48.31, 48.60, and 48.64 performances in major races. He no longer looks capable of challenging the top Brazilians or the younger Europeans/Americans. I expect him to run around 47.9-48.0.

**Matic Ian Guček rounds out the field.** The Slovenian record holder ran well with 48.03 in the European semi and 47.80 in Zürich, but he also faded to 48.76 in the European final. He is clearly improving at 22, but he does not yet have the late-season firepower of the athletes above him. A high-47 or low-48 finish seems right.
